North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed the deepening of ties with Russia in a message to President Vladimir Putin as Pyongyang marked the anniversary of independence from Japan's colonial rule, KCNA state news agency said on Sunday.
Kim was replying to a message of congratulations from Putin marking Saturday's 81st anniversary of Tokyo's surrender in World War Two. The Russian leader said the bond was forged as Soviet soldiers fought against Japan and that cooperation would continue "in all the sectors."
The North Korean leader expressed hope for the future of ties that had "carried forward the history of common struggle for justice and precious traditions of friendship."
Pyongyang and Moscow have grown closer since the reclusive state began deploying troops and weapons to support Russia's war against Ukraine in what has been Pyongyang's most significant involvement in a war since the 1950s.
The Russian ship Pallada arrived at Wonsan port for a goodwill visit on Saturday tied to the liberation anniversary, and was greeted by North Korean provincial officials and Russian embassy staff, KCNA said.
South Korean President calls for talks
Also on Saturday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for talks with the rival North aimed at peaceful coexistence, telling Seoul's Liberation Day ceremony that the two Koreas need safeguards to prevent conflict and should work to replace their armistice with a "peace regime."
Lee urged dialogue to formally end the 1950-1953 Korean War, which ended in a ceasefire but no peace treaty, and said the talks could explore ways to curb Pyongyang's nuclear program.
Pyongyang has rejected Lee's overtures and criticized US-South Korean military exercises as provocations.
On Thursday, Putin drew Tokyo's condemnation with a visit to an island off Hokkaido, claimed by Japan, that Moscow seized in the days after Japan's 1945 surrender.

articles.title: Russia’s air defense leans on a few “flying quarterback” jets
articles.body:
- Analyst Michael Bohnert says Russia has roughly half a dozen operational A-50U early warning aircraft, with no new airframes built since 1992 and no A-100 replacement in serial production.
- Analysts estimate Russia has roughly half a dozen operational A-50U aircraft, with no new airframes built since 1992 and the A-100 replacement still not in serial production.
Russia’s A-50U airborne early warning aircraft function as “flying quarterbacks” for its air defense network, and Moscow has no near-term way to replace the ones it has lost, defense researcher Michael Bohnert wrote in a recent analysis of the fleet.
Bohnert said the aircraft’s value comes down to line of sight and the curvature of the Earth. A ground-based radar can typically see a low-flying object only 10 to 20 miles away before the horizon blocks it, he said, while an airborne radar can potentially detect the same target from more than 200 miles out.
“This has two major implications,” Bohnert wrote. “The first is it provides much earlier warning. Up to an hour for a strike drone and 10 to 30 minutes for a cruise missile. The second is it covers a much larger area easily replacing a dozen or more surface radars.”
Because a single A-50U can substitute for numerous ground radars, Bohnert said Russia can leave many of those systems switched off until they are needed to target an incoming missile. A radar that is turned off, he noted, is much harder to locate because it emits no signal for enemy sensors to detect. He added that the same line-of-sight advantage extends to communications, since A-50U crews are trained to control both air and ground assets and can see and talk to nearly everything within range.
On why Russia cannot quickly rebuild the fleet, Bohnert said the last A-50 airframe was produced around 1992, and that despite periodic upgrades, the type has been out of production for decades. The base Il-76 airframe is still manufactured today, he said, but the radar system requires specialized structural reinforcements that are far harder to produce. Russia’s intended successor, the A-100, has still not entered serial production after more than a decade of development, according to Bohnert, who said the aircraft’s radar is expensive to build and depends on numerous specialized parts.
In 2025, Ukraine struck a facility involved in A-100 production using FP-1 drones, destroying a test aircraft and damaging the factory. Bohnert said work on the program has likely been on hold since, and that new aircraft are unlikely to arrive for several years.
Bohnert estimated Russia currently has around half a dozen operational A-50U aircraft, used mainly to protect Russian President Vladimir Putin and only occasionally to help Russian forces fend off increasingly frequent Ukrainian FP-1 drone and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile attacks. He pointed to Ukraine’s use of UK-supplied Storm Shadow missiles at near-maximum range inside Russian territory as an indicator of how far back from the front line the A-50U fleet is being kept.
Flight-tracking data compiled separately by the open-source channel CyberBoroshno points to the same conclusion: a small, closely guarded fleet flown under increasing pressure. The channel analyzed more than 1,600 messages referencing the A-50U between June 4 and August 2 and found the aircraft largely grounded for duty against Ukraine through June 22, aside from the return to service of a repaired airframe, tail number “47 red,” and transit flights between Vorkuta and Olenya.
Starting June 23, one aircraft began flying nearly every night over what the channel called Russia’s Volga rear area, covering Ulyanovsk and Samara regions, a pattern CyberBoroshno said held for the rest of the period and totaled roughly 60 individual sorties. The channel said an A-50U played a decisive role in repelling a Ukrainian cruise missile strike on July 4. Flights that had previously originated from Ivanovo, described as the fleet’s home base, and from Ulyanovsk largely stopped after that date, with operations dispersing to Bolshoye Savino near Perm, Orenburg-2 and Chelyabinsk, which the channel attributed to an effort to protect a scarce asset once its effectiveness became clear.
On July 7, Russia had four A-50U aircraft airborne simultaneously, which CyberBoroshno said represented nearly the entire operational fleet and a readiness level it had not previously recorded. The channel also reported one aircraft flying continuous night duty for five straight days, including a shift from 2:45 to 4:45 a.m. during which Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo missiles were in the air; Samara, one of the areas the missiles reached that night, fell within that aircraft’s coverage zone at the time.
Confirmed losses to date remain limited but are rising. The open-source monitoring project Oryx has visually confirmed the destruction of at least two A-50 aircraft and one Beriev A-100LL flying laboratory, the testbed used to develop the A-100’s radar, a figure Oryx’s methodology treats as a floor rather than a full count, since it requires photographic or video evidence for each loss.

articles.title: Trump threatens to make the Strait of Hormuz a US territory: Can he?
articles.body:
Trump threatens to make the Strait of Hormuz a US territory: Can he?
US president has yet another outlandish threat for Iran, with no end to war in sight.
President Donald Trump on Friday said he would designate the Strait of Hormuz a territory of the United States “pretty soon” as the status of the waterway, a global chokepoint through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, remains under a military and diplomatic deadlock.
Iran has fired back, dubbing Trump’s threats as “nonsense” as the memorandum of understanding signed between the two in June expires on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran says no decision yet on a return to talks with the US
- list 2 of 4Is China seeking to copy Iran’s Strait of Hormuz blockade around Taiwan?
- list 3 of 4US aircraft carrier expected to relieve USS Lincoln in Middle East
- list 4 of 4Qatar denies Tehran’s claim it is detaining Iranian bomber pilots
Tehran has blocked the passage to leverage it as a global economy kill switch, while Washington has maintained a military naval blockade against Iran’s ports, choking its economy further.
In the apparent game of who blinks first – though Trump says negotiation with Iran “is like chess” – the US president’s military rhetoric has also followed a pattern throughout the ongoing war, which began on February 28. On many occasions, he has threatened to attack Iran only to pull back at the eleventh hour.
So, can the US actually make the Strait of Hormuz its territory? And what does that even mean?
What has Trump said?
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said during a speech at a police academy in New York.
Referring to the naval blockade, Trump went a step further to suggest that the Strait of Hormuz is already a US territory. “Essentially, that’s what it is,” he added.
“We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to,” he said.
Iran maintains that it controls the waterway — and despite the US claims, some vessels have transited the passage despite the blockade, maritime navigation data shows.
“It’s clear the US president, with a chuckle as he said that, even himself, is not taking this particularly seriously,” said Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett, reporting from Washington, DC.
“These are the territorial waters of Iran and Oman. But what the US president likes to do is get under the skin of adversaries, and, in this case, it’s Iran,” she said.
“What we should point out, though, is what the US president is not backing down on is the fact that there is a naval blockade by the United States in effect in the Strait of Hormuz, and that is ongoing.
How has Iran reacted to it?
Several Iranian officials have sharply reacted to Trump’s remarks. The head of the judiciary came out with furious rhetoric, calling the US president criminal and feather-headed, his remarks “nonsense” and saying the Strait of Hormuz belongs to Iran.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, also responded, saying, “The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech.”
“The Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian; this strait will only be closed and opened under Iran’s command, and as long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and cease your fanciful delusions, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” he added.
Meanwhile, Iran has been holding talks with Oman, the only other coastal country in the strait, to reach a settlement on the management of maritime traffic in the strait. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in comments carried by the Iranian Students’ News Agency, said negotiations between Tehran and Muscat “may reach a conclusion soon”.
The reopening of the waterway, however, is a separate issue, Araghchi said, where Washington has to adhere to promises made in the June memorandum of understanding, including removal of the naval blockade and sanctions on Iran.
That is the new Iranian position on the ongoing war, where Tehran is now seeking these US concessions for mere reopening of the waterway, which were originally conditions for ending the war.
Is Trump’s claim even practical?
First, sovereignty does not exchange hands over a mere unilateral presidential proclamation.
For instance, Trump had earlier threatened to send US boots to Iran’s Kharg Island to take over the key Iranian oil export hub in the Gulf. Tehran then responded by saying that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps would be waiting for them, “with fingers on the trigger”. Trump had previously also threatened to take over Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark.
Bruce Fein, associate deputy attorney general under President Ronald Reagan, says Trump is constitutionally powerless to annex on his own.
“A treaty ratified by the Senate or statute is constitutionally required to annex territory, as with the Louisiana Purchase or annexation of Hawaii or Panama Canal or acquisition of Puerto Rico or the Philippines in ending the Spanish-American War.
If he goes ahead with annexation, Fein says, it would “constitute the crime of aggressive war under international law, including the UN Charter”.
Natalie Klein, a specialist in international law and associate dean at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, said, “Essentially the only way Trump’s claim could have any plausibility under international law would be if the US was asserting control over the Strait as an occupying power perhaps comparable to the authority the US exercised over Japan immediately after World War II.”
“But in that scenario, the US would need to have military control over Iran or at least its coastal areas.”
Trump’s war on Iran is also widely unpopular in the US, where the president and his fellow Republicans are seeking to defend their narrow congressional majorities in November’s midterm elections. Barely 35 percent of Americans approve of the war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Several US media publications have reported that Washington is running short on munitions, including the crucial Patriot antimissile interceptor. Petrol prices have also increased, and are now averaging more than $4 a gallon – a major issue for Americans.
Last week, US Vice President JD Vance said the Trump administration’s top priority in the war was to control increasing petrol prices, while stopping Iran’s supposed race to a nuclear weapon now comes second.
Tehran has also attacked its neighbours in the Gulf, which analysts say are aimed at forcing the regional countries to push Washington into a corner at the negotiating table.
Even Iran does not enjoy unfettered sovereignty over the strait as a whole, under international laws, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), but only some coastal sites near its own borders.
The UNCLOS recognises coastal-state sovereignty over territorial waters, but limits that territorial sea to 12 nautical miles (22km), and notes that ships enjoy a right of passage that “shall not be impeded”.
The Strait of Hormuz is in international waters, sandwiched between the coasts of Iran and Oman. At its narrowest point, the strait is only about 21 nautical miles (39km) wide — and the two countries’ 12-nautical mile territorial seas overlap across it.
While neither the US nor Iran has ratified UNCLOS, the convention’s rules on international straits are widely regarded as customary law.
Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, said Trump usually makes such statements primarily to speak to a US audience, especially his support base.
It is important to remember, he added, that Trump is a product of US reality TV and is, at the end of the day, a “showman”.
“This is a guy who speaks big. You have to take him seriously in some cases but not literally,” Musgrave cautioned.
Trump cannot be taken seriously, especially in this case because making the strait US territory is physically and legally impossible, he said. But the statements do show that Trump is determined not to back down from Iran and accept defeat in the months-long war, he added.

articles.title: The Russian Federation attacked Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih with missiles and 106 drones, the Air Force reports
articles.body:
The Russian Federation attacked Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih with missiles and 106 drones, the Air Force reports
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of August 16, Russian forces struck Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih. Air defense forces shot down 85 UAVs and three Kh-59/69 missiles.
During the night of August 16, Russian forces attacked Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih with Oniks anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, as well as 106 Shahed-type strike UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera UAVs and Parody-type decoy drones. This was reported by UNN, citing the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Details
The strikes were launched from the Kursk, Bryansk, Belgorod and Voronezh regions; the cities of Kursk, Millerovo, Oryol, Bryansk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk; as well as the occupied parts of Donetsk, Kherson and Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Air defense shot down/suppressed three Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, as well as 85 enemy Shahed- and Gerbera-type UAVs and drones of other types in the north, south, east and center of the country. Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three locations
As a reminder
Over the course of August 15, Russian forces lost 1,510 soldiers in the war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian Drone Strike on Car in Sumy Kills Man, Injures Woman
articles.body:
A Russian drone struck a civilian vehicle in the northeastern city of Sumy late Saturday, Aug. 15, killing a 59-year-old man and injuring his wife.
Sumy Regional Military Administration Head Oleh Hryhorov reported the attack on Telegram, stating the drone targeted the car, causing it to catch fire.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The deceased victim’s wife was hospitalized with injuries and is receiving medical care.
Hryhorov noted that Russian forces repeatedly attacked Sumy with drones throughout the evening and night. While Ukrainian air defenses intercepted some of the targets, he emphasized that the overall intensity of the attacks remained high.
Strikes on Kryvyi Rih and Kyiv
The attack on Sumy occurred alongside a broader wave of Russian strikes early Sunday morning, Aug. 16.
Russian forces launched a combined attack using ballistic missiles and drones against Kryvyi Rih in the Dnipropetrovsk region. The strikes killed one person and injured 13 others. A 48-year-old man was hospitalized in severe condition, while 10 others were admitted in moderate condition.
The strikes damaged two industrial enterprises and ignited fires. Separate attacks in the Nikopol district injured a 55-year-old man and damaged local infrastructure and residential buildings.
Concurrently, Russian forces attacked Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, with ballistic missiles. The State Emergency Service reported that the strikes caused fires and structural damage in the Obolonskyi and Holosiivskyi districts, injuring three people.

In the Obolonskyi district, a large fire broke out at a local market, and falling debris ignited several parked vehicles. In the Holosiivskyi district, rescue workers contained a fire that started in a non-residential development zone following the strikes.

articles.title: Iran, US trade Hormuz threats; Hamas in Cairo for Gaza talks
articles.body:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in the Middle East.
Here are the key events on Sunday morning:
• Iran and the US are continuing to sabre-rattle over the Strait of Hormuz. Trump on Saturday claimed he could declare the strategic waterway a "territory of the United States" while a senior Iranian diplomat told the US to "accept the reality of defeat".
• The threats come ahead of Monday's deadline under the June Islamabad agreement, which gave the US and Iran two months to reach an understanding on reopening the key waterway.
• Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Oman over the strait are continuing but that re-opening the waterway is a "completely separate matter" that will depend on the US meeting Tehran's conditions.
• Qatar has denied claims by Iran that it is holding three pilots captured during a combat mission earlier in the war.
• Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya is in Cairo for talks with mediators over the Board of Peace's Gaza plan rejected by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump envoy Jared Kushner will visit Israel and Egypt next week in a bid to rescue the deal.
• Israel has threatened to further escalate attacks on Lebanon, a day after killing at least 11 people in one of the heaviest rounds of strikes since the ceasefire came into effect in June.
UK minister condemns West Bank 'settler terrorism'
UK Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty has condemned the ongoing wave of settler violence in the occupied West Bank
"I am horrified at the scenes we are seeing yet again in recent days in the West Bank and the shocking surge in settler violence," he said in a video statement on X.
"Settler violence and settler terrorism are appalling and must end," he said, calling on the Israeli government to prevent further anti-Palestinian violence.
Doughty's comments came on the back of international outrage at the besieging of Palestinians in the village of Qusra, where the Israeli military enabled a days-long siege of civilian homes by settler militants.
Hamas chief in Cairo for Gaza talks ahead of Kushner visit
Hamas political chief Khalil al-Hayya in in Cairo for talks with Egyptian officials ahead of a visit by US President Donald Trump's envoy Jared Kushner to the region.
Hayya, who is visiting Egypt for the first time since assuming leadership of Hamas in late July, was expected to meet with Egypt's intelligence chief Hassan Rashad on Sunday morning, the source said.
Kushner will visit Israel and Egypt next week in a bid to rescue the Trump-backed Board of Peace's Gaza plan rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
He will be accompanied by Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's Gaza envoy.
Yemeni government forces said Sunday that Houthi fighters have launched new missile and drone attacks on the port city of Mocha.
Air defences had intercepted a drone fired by the group, they said.
The director of Mocha port said Saturday it has been forced to suspend operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in recent days.
The recent attacks have raised fears that Yemen could be sliding back into civil war, four years after a ceasefire ended the conflict between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.
The head of Iran's parliamentary national security committee, Ebrahim Azizi, has mocked Trump over his latest threats to take over the Strait of Hormuz.
"The US President ought to worry about his own security rather than his endless bluffing regarding the Strait of Hormuz; before he ends up hiding in a food truck," Azizi wrote on X on Saturday.
He was referring to reports in US media that Trump hid in a catering truck to leave Air Force One during a recent visit to Turkey following concerns about an Iranian attack.
Iran executes man over involvement in January protests
Iran's judiciary announced the execution on Sunday of a man who was convicted of running over several police officers with his car during anti-government protests in January.
"Shahram Sadeghi, sentenced to death for having carried out an operational action in support of the Zionist regime and the United States, was executed this morning," the judiciary's Mizan Online website said.
It added that the man had run over several police officers with his car on 8 January in Karaj, west of Tehran, wounding seven of them.
A protest movement initially sparked in late December by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 January.
Israel threatens escalation in Lebanon amid new strike
Lebanese media reported a new Israeli attack in the south on Sunday shortly after Israel's defence minister Israel Katz vowed to continue strikes.
Lebanon's National News Agency reported in a strike in Majdal Zoun on Sunday morning, a day after at least 11 people were killed in the heaviest Israeli attacks since the US-brokered ceasefire came into effect in June.
"No account in any arena will remain open. We will defend our soldiers and civilians with force," Katz wrote on X.
Medics at the site of an Israeli strike in Deir al-Zahrani, 15 August 2026. [Getty]
Iran disputes Qatar, Kuwait accounts of captured pilots
An Iranian military official said on Sunday that Qatar should allow an Iranian team to enter the country to investigate the fate of pilots whom Tehran says were captured by Qatari forces, Iranian media reported.
Qatar denies holding any Iranian pilots. Doha said on Saturday that its search and rescue teams had found the remains of one pilot after Iranian aircraft violated Qatari airspace in March and failed to respond to attempts to contact them.
Qatar said it had contacted Iran to coordinate the handover of the remains and had invited Tehran to review details of its search and rescue operations, but had received no response.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said an Iranian Air Force expert and fact-finding team had been waiting for months to enter Qatar, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
He accused Qatari officials of repeatedly delaying the investigation and preventing the pilots' return to Iran. He called for the International Committee of the Red Cross to urgently follow up on the case.

articles.title: Why Iran’s threat keeps haunting the Middle East - and how to finally break the cycle - opinion
articles.body:
For nearly 50 years, the world has dealt with Iran under a straightforward premise: the sole source of danger is the theocracy installed by the 1979 revolution.
Western policies have split between containing the regime, changing its conduct, eroding its capabilities, or waiting for internal collapse. The record of these tactics, though, raises a tougher question.
Why does the Iranian threat return each time Tehran’s foes believe they have contained it?
The breeding grounds enabling centralized power
For decades, the world may have fixated on who governs Iran while ignoring the framework that lets central authorities rebuild their power project whenever conditions change.
The core issue is about more than the nuclear program, ballistic missile stockpile, and proxy networks. These are assets that can be disabled or partly destroyed.
They spring, however, from a large state with a huge population, energy reserves, a scientific and industrial foundation, geographic reach, and military institutions honed across decades.
Lost facilities, leaders, and munitions cannot wipe out technical know-how or erase recovery capacity. A single tool may break, but the underlying machine still can build a replacement.
History shows international dealings with Iran have targeted what can be destroyed; capabilities can be degraded. But such tactics leave unanswered the more fundamental question of how to stop a large, centralized state with people, resources and expertise from rebuilding losses once conditions ease.
So, the issue moves from disarmament to state structure, from who governs Iran to how power sources inside the country are administered.
One episode lays bare this disconnect. The July 2015 nuclear deal capped portions of Iran’s nuclear work. It left Tehran’s view of its regional standing intact. Missile work and proxy operations also proceeded without pause.
The January 2020 killing of Maj.-Gen. Qasem Soleimani jolted the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, although influence networks resumed activity once roles were reassigned.
Strikes on Iranian military sites have proved able to inflict damage and disrupt operations, but they cannot ensure permanent disablement.
Containment thus amounts to little more than managing repeated rounds of buildup, strike and rearmament.
Viewed this way, regime change in Iran offers at best a partial fix if presented as a final answer to the problem. The ruling system provides the country’s power project with its ideology, while the centralized state furnishes its resources and wealth.
Replacing the regime while leaving power administration untouched may soften rhetoric but offers no assurance of a different course. A more pragmatic, economy-focused government could emerge.
Geography, national interests and latent capabilities, however, survive leadership turnover. Long-held regional ambitions would likely resurface, framed in nationalist rather than revolutionary terms.
That said, casting the Iranian state as inherently hostile misreads reality. Most countries adjust conduct when their institutions, military doctrine, and balance between rulers and ruled evolve.
The objective is something other than indefinite weakening of Iran. It is blocking the convergence of unchecked central power, expansionist ideology, and exclusive control over military decisions.
Chaotic breakup of the Iranian state carries its own severe risks. Internal diversity, widespread weapons, and Iran’s strategic position could turn collapse into civil conflict, foreign meddling, and massive disruption of energy flows and shipping lanes.
Break the ‘buildup, strike, resurgence’ pattern
The most durable course therefore starts inside Iran, on the premise that Iranians alone hold the right to choose their governing system and its structure.
Broad decentralization or federalism, and possibly confederal arrangements if adopted through national consent and constitutional agreement, can curb the center’s monopoly on wealth and decisions, give regions greater say over resources and fiscal matters, and write institutional limits into the use of national capacities for foreign ventures.
Forcing such models from outside, by contrast, would let authorities cast themselves as defenders of national unity and turn reform into a pretext for harsher repression.
Decentralization hardly guarantees Iran will turn automatically into a peaceful country. Constitutional arrangements by themselves cannot dispel national ambitions or remove foreign frictions. Their worth lies in raising the price of decision monopolization, spreading oversight of resources, and making long-term foreign ventures far harder to pursue without broad consent and accountability.
Such rules constrain impulsive action while still falling short of an ironclad promise of responsible behavior.
No global requirement exists for a permanent Iranian adversary to justify alliances and defense budgets. Removing the regime with no plan for what follows promises an even more dangerous crisis.
What is required instead is ending the threat’s ability to regenerate, through four parallel steps: capping offensive capabilities, advancing institutional reform that disperses power inside Iran, upholding regional deterrence to block coercion, and pursuing diplomacy that links economic and political integration to revised conduct.
The world has repeatedly slowed Iran’s power project. It has never eliminated the country’s ability to rebuild it. The ruling system may fall one day, but its collapse would leave intact the building blocks of Iranian strength.
If a framework survives that lets central authorities marshal people, resources and expertise behind foreign ventures, any win will amount to a temporary pause between rounds.
A credible resolution comes when Iran’s strength changes from a source of fear for neighbors into a force bounded by institutions and directed by societal interests. Only then does the root problem resolve itself. The danger will not have sustained another setback – it will have lost the conditions that kept reviving it.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Devastate Metinvest’s Zaporizhstal Factory, Epicentr Mall in Zaporizhzhia

Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia have severely damaged two major Ukrainian businesses, forcing a complete shutdown of Metinvest’s Zaporizhstal steel plant and destroying an Epicentr shopping center. articles.title: U.S. Air Force buys Chinese-made drones for nuclear missile base
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force is buying DJI drones for F.E. Warren AFB to train missile security forces against the type of foreign drones they are most likely to encounter.
- The brand-name justification cites DJI's 80 to 85 percent global market share and says the drones will run modified "RIZER" software to block data transfer before use.
The U.S. Air Force is buying Chinese-made DJI drones for a Wyoming nuclear missile base, using the foreign aircraft as stand-ins for the kind of drones security forces there are training to detect and shoot down.
The 90th Contracting Squadron posted a combined synopsis and solicitation on August 14 seeking a small business vendor to supply the drones for F.E. Warren Air Force Base, home to the 90th Missile Security Operations Squadron and part of Air Force Global Strike Command. Quotes are due August 24, with questions due five days earlier. The squadron says it needs the aircraft to run counter-small unmanned aircraft systems training, exercises meant to test radar, jamming and other defeat systems against real drone signals rather than simulated ones.
The order calls for two DJI Mavic 2 Pro quadcopters with Fly More kits, listed as refurbished, two DJI Mini 3 Pro drones with remote controllers, two DJI Avata 2 Fly More combos and six airdrop payload release devices, plus shipping. The government intends to award a firm fixed price contract to the lowest-priced offer that meets the technical requirements, according to the solicitation.
Contracting officials designated the purchase a brand-name requirement, meaning DJI specifically, rather than an open competition among drone makers. A justification document signed July 29 by Contracting Officer Chad A. Evans, a technical sergeant, states that DJI controls an estimated 80 to 85 percent of the global commercial drone market and that its “highly distinct, proprietary electronic protocols, radio frequency (RF) signatures, and flight capabilities” are not replicated by American-made drones or other manufacturers.
“To properly test our counter-systems and train our operators against the most statistically probable real-world threat, the 90 MSOS must utilize the exact devices adversaries are most likely to employ,” the justification states.
The document warns that without the specific DJI hardware, the squadron’s “no-fail nuclear security mission” would be degraded. Relying only on computer-simulated data or U.S.-made drones, the justification argues, would leave operators untested against DJI’s actual radio signatures and communication protocols, creating what it calls a critical blind spot in installation defense.
F.E. Warren is one of three U.S. Air Force bases that operates Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, and its security forces are responsible for defending that missile field against ground and airborne threats. The justification states that Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, another Global Strike Command missile base, is pursuing or using similar DJI platforms for its own counter-drone training, and frames the F.E. Warren purchase as bringing the two installations toward standardized threat replication across the command’s missile fields.
The document cites a Secretary of War memo titled “Unleashing U.S. Military Drone Dominance” as the legal authority permitting officers at the rank of O-6, or colonel, and equivalent to procure small quantities of foreign drone equipment for electronic warfare testing, training and counter-UAS development. That authority falls under 10 U.S.C. 2304(c)(1), which allows agencies to solicit from a single source under specific circumstances rather than through full and open competition.
To address cybersecurity concerns tied to Chinese-manufactured hardware, the justification says every DJI aircraft purchased will be loaded with software called RIZER before operational use. The document describes RIZER as overriding the drones’ native firmware to create what it calls “a completely air-gapped system that cannot transfer or download telemetry or imagery to foreign entities or DoW networks.”
The justification also states that the squadron identified multiple authorized DJI resellers and distributors capable of meeting the brand-name requirement, allowing the procurement to proceed as a 100 percent small business set-aside rather than a true single-source award to one company.

articles.title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
articles.body:
Russia has lost around 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 16.
The figure includes 1,510 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,270 tanks, 25,151 armored combat vehicles, 134,851 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,007 artillery systems, 2,034 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,570 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 463,404 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,257 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

articles.title: Iran says Qatar delaying probe into fate of Iranian pilots, Tasnim news agency
articles.body:
Iran accuses Qatar of thwarting probe into fate of pilots
- Iran said the airmen have been held since March 2 when their fighter jets were shot down.
- Qatar denies holding the pilots, saying it invited Iran for briefings on rescue efforts but that Tehran did not respond.
- The incident ties into a wider Middle East conflict involving US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with ongoing tensions and failed peace talks.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran accused Qatar on Aug 16 of thwarting efforts to work out what happened to three pilots Tehran says were captured during the Middle East war, though the Gulf state has denied detaining them.
Iran previously reported that one pilot was killed and others missing after a sortie to Qatar in March, but did not claim at the time that any of them was captured.
“A team of experts from the Iranian Air Force has been waiting for several months to travel to Qatar to conduct an on-site investigation,” said Iranian General Mohammad Bagherzadeh.
“However, due to persistent delays by Qatari authorities, the return of our brave pilots to their homeland remains impossible,” he added, according to the Tasnim news agency.
He called on Doha to authorise the team to travel to Qatar.
Bagherzadeh accused Qatar on Aug 15 of having captured three Iranian pilots who were carrying out an operation against the United States’ Al Udeid air base in early March and demanded their release.
Qatar denied holding the pilots and said an invitation was sent to Iran “to be briefed on the details of the search & rescue operations in April, but the Iranian side has yet to respond”.
Iran’s military said in July it retrieved the body of pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during the attack on Al Udeid.
The largest US military base in the Middle East, Al Udeid hosts forward elements of US Central Command, as well as its air and special operations forces.
In early March, Qatar’s Defence Ministry said it shot down two Iranian Sukhoi Su-24 bombers.
It was not immediately clear whether they were the same aircraft referred to by Iran, as Qatar and other countries across the region faced retaliatory attacks following the US and Israeli strikes that triggered the war.
It was the first time a Gulf country reported shooting down an Iranian aircraft since the war broke out on Feb 28.
The Middle East war broke out when the US and Israel attacked Iran, which retaliated with attacks across the region.
Diplomatic efforts led to an April ceasefire that ended nearly 40 days of fighting, followed by the signing of a framework for peace talks in June that later collapsed.
Iran and the US have since traded fire sporadically, with fighting mainly centred in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar, which took part in mediation efforts to end the fighting, came under fire after the truce broke down, reporting attacks on its territory and at least one Qatari tanker transiting the strait. AFP

articles.title: Ukrainian rapper mocked Russia’s claim he helped deliver drones for attacks near Moscow. A month later, Russia allegedly tried to kill him in Poland
articles.body:
On 14 August 2026, Polish broadcaster RMF FM identified American-Ukrainian rapper and video blogger Kyivstoner as the previously unnamed target of an alleged Russian-directed assassination plot in Warsaw. The case comes as European authorities investigate suspected Russian attacks and sabotage across the continent.
The alleged plot against Kyivstoner comes amid attacks on Kremlin critics abroad, including the fatal shooting of a Russian opposition artist in Poland in June.
Polish authorities disclosed the Kyivstoner's case on 13 August but withheld the target’s identity. RMF’s identification points to a possible motive, though it relies on unverified allegations from the FSB, Russia's domestic security agency that Kyivstoner of managed drone deliveries intended for attacks near Moscow.
Who is Kyivstoner?
Kyivstoner was born Albert Vasiliev and uses the name Slevin Dadyan on his US passport. He gained attention through humorous videos and the Ukrainian group Hryby before releasing solo tracks, including “Leto” (Summer) and “Zvuk” (Sound).
In a 2025 interview, Vasiliev voiced support for Ukrainians and opposition to Russian occupation, saying Russian ruler Vladimir Putin made him angry and that he wanted civilians and soldiers to stop dying.
In July 2026, Russia’s FSB accused Kyivstoner of overseeing logistics for a foiled drone attack on a defense enterprise near Moscow.
The agency alleged that 35 drones assembled in Kyiv were concealed in a shipment of ceramic tiles and smuggled into Russia through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus. Russian authorities also added Vasiliev to a register of people they label as involved in extremist or terrorist activity.
Vasiliev responded on Instagram by mocking Russia's allegation, saying he had been relaxing and playing video games rather than organizing an attack.
Russian authorities also accuse him of cooperating with Ukrainian intelligence. He denies the accusations, and RMF offered no independent evidence to substantiate them.
Suspect detained before alleged attack
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Polish services detained the Russian suspect on 7 August, stopping the alleged attack “at the last minute.” US services assisted the operation. A Polish court remanded the man in custody for three months.
The journalists described the Russian citizen as a native of Donbas in eastern Ukraine. Tusk said the target, who holds Ukrainian and US passports, was “inconvenient to the Putin regime.”
The prime minister called it the first Russian-ordered attempt of its kind against a US citizen in another NATO country.
Killings and disrupted plots across Europe
Throughout Europe, Russia has tried to hunt down and kill anti-Kremlin critics and supporters of Ukraine. In June, Russian opposition artist Robert Kuzovkov, known as Semyon Skrepetsky, was shot dead in eastern Poland. Hours earlier, he had reported threats from “Russian patriots.” Polish authorities detained two Belarusian nationals, but have not attributed the killing to Moscow.
US and German services also reportedly foiled a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger in 2024. German intelligence later treated the surveillance of Bavarian drone manufacturer Donaustahl’s CEO as a suspected planned assassination.

articles.title: Ukraine hit the plant that fuels Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S rockets Russia fires at frontline cities with no metro to shelter in
articles.body:
Ukraine struck the plant that fuels the rockets Russia rains on its frontline cities. On the night of 16 August 2026, Ukraine's Defense Forces hit an important Russian military-industrial enterprise, the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast, and a fire was recorded at the site, the General Staff reported.
The plant makes the fuel for weapons that Russia uses to grind down Ukrainian civilian areas. The Kamensky Combine produces solid rocket fuel for the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, which Russia fires at frontline cities like Zaporizhzhia, where there is no metro to shelter in and civilians have only minutes to get behind walls the rockets punch through easily.
The Tornado-S is one of Russia’s most advanced long-range rocket artillery systems, capable of striking targets up to 120 kilometers away. Russian “Tornado-S” and “Smerch” systems are designed to fire and retreat rapidly, making them extremely difficult to locate.
The target feeds Russia's rocket artillery
The Kamensky Combine is a node in Russia's weapons production. It produces solid rocket fuel for the rocket systems, as well as a range of missile systems and aviation strike weapons, with its output directly serving the needs of Russia's armed forces.
The damage is still being assessed. The extent of the damage and the results of the strike are being clarified, the General Staff said, with a fire confirmed at the site.
Two earlier strikes were confirmed hit
The General Staff also confirmed results from recent deep strikes. Analysis of additional data confirmed the shutdown of the ZapSibNeftekhim complex in Tobolsk, Tyumen Oblast, one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, after its central gas-fractionation unit was struck on 10 August.
A refinery was confirmed to have been hit, too. The 11 August strike at the Orsknaftaorgsyntez refinery in Orsk, Orenburg Oblast, damaged its hydrocracking unit, several primary oil-processing units, and a secondary distillation unit. The refinery produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, and other products for Russia's armed forces and military industry.
The campaign continues
The General Staff signaled more to come. Work on key military and military-industrial targets of the enemy continues, it said, closing with "to be continued."
That promise fits a campaign that has spent 2026 reaching ever deeper into Russia, hitting the refineries, petrochemical plants, and now rocket-fuel factories that supply the war. Each confirmed strike degrades a different piece of Russia's ability to produce the weapons and fuel its forces run on.

Mohammed Sameai and Serdar Dincel

The Houthi group launched a new wave of drone and missile attacks in Mocha and Marib in southwestern Yemen as escalation continues to rise in the war-torn Arab country, according to pro-government forces and local media on Sunday.
The National Resistance Forces, aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and led by Presidential Leadership Council member Tariq Saleh, said one missile hit Mocha, without giving details about injuries or damage.
In Marib, the provincial government’s media office said six ballistic missiles and four drones targeted residential neighborhoods in the city Saturday evening, injuring four people and causing damage to homes and civilian property.
A statement by the media office said one strike hit a bakery in the Al-Sharika neighborhood north of Marib city, wounding one person.
Strikes also targeted several neighborhoods in the densely populated city, damaging vehicles and homes, the statement said.
The media office called on the international community to “condemn these attacks and crimes targeting displacement camps, residential neighborhoods and civilian facilities, and document them as violations of international humanitarian law.”
The Houthis have not yet commented on the report.
Mocha and Marib have come under repeated Houthi attacks in recent days amid mounting escalation across the war-torn country.
Yemen has witnessed a relative lull since April 2022 in a war that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and other cities and provinces since September 2014.
Fighting has resumed in several provinces in recent weeks, including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea and Taiz, as the country continues to face one of the world’s worst humanitarian and economic crises.

articles.title: Spanish F-18 shoots down drone over Romania
articles.body:
- A Spanish F-18 on NATO air policing duty shot down a drone over Romania near Galați at 5:01 a.m. Sunday, the fourth such intercept this year.
- The drone entered from Moldova, and its wreckage fell in an unpopulated area between Băleni and Cudalbi with no reported injuries or damage.
A Spanish F-18 fighter jet flying NATO air policing duty shot down a drone that crossed into Romanian airspace early Sunday, marking the fourth drone Romania has shot down this year, the country’s Ministry of National Defence said.
Romanian radar systems detected the aircraft entering national airspace at 4:44 a.m. local time, arriving from neighboring Moldova about 24 km (15 miles) north of Galați. Two Spanish F-18s from the Spanish Air and Space Force, already on alert as a precaution, were dispatched from the 57th Air Base “Mihail Kogălniceanu.” One of the jets established radar contact with the target and received approval to engage. The drone was shot down safely at 5:01 a.m.
“The drone was shot down safely at 05:01 am,” the ministry said.
The ministry did not identify the drone’s origin. A possible impact point for the wreckage was located between the villages of Băleni and Cudalbi in Galați County, in an area the ministry described as unpopulated. The air alert for Galați County was lifted at 5:20 a.m. No injuries or property damage were reported.
Romania’s defense minister, Radu Miruta, confirmed the intercept and credited both the Spanish pilots and the Romanian command center personnel who tracked the incursion, according to Euronews. Miruta said Romania is defending its airspace with the backing of its NATO allies, pointing to the country’s roughly 614-km (382-mile) land border with Ukraine as the reason it sits on what he called the front line of the alliance’s eastern defenses.
The incident is the fourth time Romania has shot down a drone this year. In July, Romanian F-16 pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace, the first time the country had taken that step since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. Earlier this year, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați during an overnight attack on targets across the border in Ukraine, injuring two people.
Romania has scrambled fighter jets in response to airspace incursions multiple times in recent months. Two Spanish F-18s were sent up last Thursday after an airborne object was detected near the river border with Ukraine; that drone spent about 12 minutes over Romanian territory before returning to Ukraine, prompting an SMS alert to residents of Tulcea County. A day later, a separate drone crossed into Romania undetected by radar because it was flying at very low altitude, according to Euronews.
Airspace violations have also been reported elsewhere along NATO’s eastern flank. On Friday, NATO said Italian fighter jets on its air policing mission shot down a drone that had entered Latvian airspace near Balvi. Poland and the Baltic states have reported similar breaches tied to Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Romania’s parliament passed legislation this year authorizing its military to destroy, neutralize or take control of unidentified aircraft that illegally enter its airspace. The bill followed repeated incidents of Russian drones crossing into or crashing on Romanian territory since 2022. Gheorghita Vlad, Romania’s defense chief, had previously called for legal changes to give the military that authority.
The Ministry of National Defence said it is continuing to monitor the situation and is briefing allied structures in real time. The investigation into the drone’s origin and the cause of the incursion remains ongoing.

Russian forces have completed the deployment of 16 launchers for jet-powered attack drones at the Tsymbulova drone base in Russia’s Oryol region, while satellite imagery also shows more than 100 drones stored in the open at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Strategic Aviation on August 15, the new infrastructure includes 10 launchers designed for Geran-5 drones and six for Geran-4 UAVs. The work was completed over roughly one month.
The facility also contains four launchers for Geran-3 drones and three launchers for the more widely used Geran-2, the Russian designation for Shahed-type attack drones.

Russia has additionally installed nearly 100 solar panels across the site. According to Strategic Aviation, they are intended to provide supplementary power for communications equipment, weather stations, and drone guidance systems, increasing the facility’s ability to continue operating during possible power disruptions.
The Tsymbulova drone base is located near the village of Tsymbulova in Russia’s Oryol region, approximately 175–180 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
The expansion comes as Russia increases production of its newer jet-powered attack drones. articles.title: World Archery just reinstated Russia’s flag and anthem, despite its killing more than 760 Ukrainian athletes and coaches since 2022
articles.body:
An international sports body has welcomed Russia back under its flag while Russia keeps killing Ukraine's athletes and civilians. The World Archery Federation has lifted restrictions on Russian athletes, allowing them to compete with their country's identity, including under the Russian flag and anthem, the federation announced.
Russia has killed more than 760 Ukrainian athletes and coaches since the start of the full-scale war, with many others made refugees or losing loved ones to strikes on civilians, and some who took up arms without combat experience. Among them is Ukrainian archer Oleksandr Onyshchuk, a master of sport and European champion, killed fighting the occupiers.
What World Archery decided
The federation acted on an Olympic ruling. Its Executive Board met online on 14 August to review the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) 7 July decision, which confirmed that earlier recommendations restricting Russian athletes no longer applied, then lifted the restrictions on Russian athletes, teams, and officials at its events.
The Russians may now compete fully. They can take part under their national flag and anthem at events including the Archery World Cup and World Championships, and the 2022 restrictions on the Russian flag and anthem were removed, in line with a similar decision on Belarus in May. The federation said participation remains subject to standard eligibility, anti-doping, host-country, and visa requirements, and that it supports the Ukrainian archery community and all affected by the war.
Ukraine calls it sportswashing
For Ukraine, the reinstatement serves Russia's propaganda. Allowing Russian athletes into international competition is a means of sportswashing, spreading disinformation, and legitimizing the aggression against Ukraine before foreign audiences, while presenting Russia as still part of the civilized world.
Ukraine also points to who Russia sends. Ukrainian intelligence has documented Russian athletes who are direct participants in the war, including a lieutenant colonel in Russia's armed forces and a deputy brigade commander who competed internationally, according to Ukraine's Defense Intelligence.
Ukraine's National Olympic Committee called the IOC decision behind the reinstatement premature and unjustified and has appealed it to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The archery ruling arrives as Russia's strikes keep killing Ukrainian civilians and athletes in the war that the returning competitors' flag represents.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills civilian in Moscow region – governor
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone attack kills civilian in Moscow region – governor
An 83-year old man died and six more people were injured as a result of an overnight Ukrainian drone strike in Moscow Region, local governor Andrey Vorobyev has said, adding that electronic warfare shot down or intercepted 287 Ukrainian UAVs.
The strike comes as Kiev has intensified long-range attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and residential areas. Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone struck a crowded beach in the southern resort of Gelendzhik, killing at least seven people, including three children, and injuring dozens more.
Drones were intercepted over Domodedovo, Podolsk, Stupino, Odintsovo, Naro-Fominsk, Ramenskoye, Chekhov, Kolomna, Kashira, and Yegoryevsk, Vorobyev said on Sunday in a post on Telegram.
The governor said that the 83-year-old man was killed when a drone fell on the grounds of a private house. Three people were injured in Podolsk as a truck driver suffered a hand injury in Klimovsk. Another man sustained shrapnel wounds at the Lesnoy allotment association, where a private house was also damaged, while a woman in the settlement of Zheleznodorozhny suffered a shoulder injury. None of the injuries were life-threatening, Vorobyev added.
Several homes and a shopping center were damaged in Domodedovo, where a balcony also caught fire. A private house and a church school were damaged in Chekhov, while a bathhouse was destroyed in Stupino, Vorobyev noted.
A storage facility linked to e-commerce giant Wildberries caught fire after a drone strike in the Koledino industrial park in Podolsk, while a warehouse storing medicines caught fire in Domodedovo. Damage was also reported at a newly built police department in Kashira and at industrial facilities in Voskresensk. A power line was damaged in the Matveyevskoye cottage settlement, the governor specified.
Wildberries press office confirmed the fire at its warehouse in Podolsk, saying that the facility had been evacuated and deliveries rerouted to other sites.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported on Sunday that 822 Ukrainian drones were destroyed over Russian regions and the Black and Azov seas. Five people were killed in the Rostov Region, while attacks also injured civilians in Belgorod and Bryansk regions. Damage was reported in several regions, including to homes, public buildings, and industrial facilities. In Belgorod, a drone attack on a civilian bus killed one woman and injured nine more people.
Russian authorities have condemned Kiev’s drone raids as terrorist attacks targeting civilians. In May, a triple wave of Ukrainian UAV strikes on a student dormitory in Donbass’ Starobelsk killed 21 people, mostly teenage girls, and partially collapsed the five-storey building.
Russia has responded to the raids by stepping up its long-range missile and drone strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial and logistical infrastructure. Moscow maintains that it never targets civilians, only military sites and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania
articles.body:
A Spanish F-18 fighter jet on a NATO air-policing mission Sunday shot down a drone that had illegally entered Romanian airspace.
The drone was detected by radar about 24 kilometers north of the eastern city of Galați after entering Romania from Moldova. Having established radar contact, the fighter jet was authorized to shoot it down at 5:01 a.m. Authorities said debris from the destroyed aircraft had fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages.
Martin O'Donnell, spokesperson for NATO operation headquarters, said additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remained under investigation but that the drone "appears to be Russian.”
Advertisement
"The Ministry of National Defence is constantly monitoring the situation and informs in real time the allied structures about such events," the ministry added in a statement.
It is the fourth drone shot down by NATO over Romania since the beginning of 2026. In July, Romanian F-16s downed three Russian drones that breached the country's airspace — the first such interceptions after dozens of incursions since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați, injuring two people.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine traded strikes over the weekend. Russian forces launched missile and drone attacks on Kyiv early Sunday, sparking fires in at least two districts and injuring three people, according to the city's military administration.
Ukrainian drones also struck the Moscow region overnight in what the regional governor Andrei Vorobyov described as one of the largest attacks to target the area, killing an 83-year-old man.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with missiles and drones: strikes and falling debris recorded at 16 locations
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine with missiles and drones: strikes and falling debris recorded at 16 locations
Russia attacked Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih with various types of missiles and launched 106 drones across Ukraine on the night of 15-16 August. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: Russian forces used Oniks anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, as well as Shahed-type attack UAVs, including jet-powered versions, Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoy drones.
The main targets of the attack were Kyiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
Early reports indicate that as of 08:00, Ukrainian air defence had shot down or jammed 85 Russian drones and three Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles.
The Air Force recorded strikes by Russian aerial weapons at 13 locations. Debris from downed aerial assets fell at three other locations.
The attack was still ongoing at the time of the report, with several Russian drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.
Background: On the night of 15-16 August, Russian forces launched a combined ballistic missile and UAV attack on Kryvyi Rih, killing one person and injuring 13 others.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Last Shadow T200 Interceptor Drone, Exceeding Expected Range
articles.body:
Ukraine has tested a new interceptor drone capable of flying more than 120 kilometers (74 miles) as Kyiv seeks cheaper ways to destroy Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) targeting its cities and front lines.
The ‘Last Shadow T200’ reached 122 kilometers (76 miles) during recent combat trials, well beyond the 70-kilometer (43-mile) range originally expected, developer Ukrainska Bavovna told Ukrainian defense news outlet Militarnyi.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The aircraft maintained a stable video link throughout the test, according to the company, potentially expanding the distance over which Ukrainian forces can operate the interceptor.
The T200 is designed to defend cities and operate along the frontline against targets including Shahed and Geran attack drones, Gerbera decoys and Molniya drones, company representatives told Militarnyi.
It has a stated top speed of 300 kilometers (186 miles) per hour, can operate at altitudes of up to 16,400 feet (4,999 meters) and can remain airborne for about an hour at cruising speed.
Ukrainska Bavovna began developing the interceptor last year, and both the airframe and its warhead have been approved for use by Ukraine’s defense ministry.
Anti-spoofing defense
The aircraft is equipped with a movable camera designed to improve target detection.
Its video system can also switch between channels and frequency bands to counter Shtora, a Russian system designed to disrupt or spoof drone video feeds.
Russian Strikes Devastate Metinvest’s Zaporizhstal Factory, Epicentr Mall in Zaporizhzhia
Developers are also integrating an automatic terminal-guidance system that would allow an operator to lock onto a target before handing off the final stage of the interception to the drone.
The airframe is produced using 3D printing, but the manufacturer plans to shift to casting within several months to improve durability and allow the aircraft to be reused after multiple landings.
Leader in drone warfare
Ukraine has rapidly expanded itsdomestic drone industry since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, developing everything from long-range strike machines to increasingly sophisticated interceptors.
Interceptor drones now account for around 40% of Ukraine’s kills of Russian Shahed-type drones and other long-range attack UAVs.

articles.title: Massive Overnight Ukrainian Drone Strikes Target Moscow Region
articles.body:
A series of drone attacks targeted the Moscow and Rostov regions overnight into August 16, causing fires at several warehouses and resulting in casualties.
In the city of Podolsk, a drone strike caused a fire at a Wildberries warehouse in the Koledino industrial park, Moscow region governor Andrei Vorobyov said.
Vorobyov said all employees had been evacuated and that none were injured. Videos showed a large fire at the site being tackled by helicopters. The Koledino facility is one of Wildberries' largest warehouses.
The facility has been repeatedly targeted in a wider campaign against Wildberries warehouses across Russia since mid-July. Reuters reported in late July that at least seven of the retailer's warehouses had been damaged in a matter of days, while AP said more than a dozen facilities had been attacked by early August.
Ukrainian authorities allege that the e-commerce company’s warehouses are involved in supplying Russian military needs. Wildberries and the Kremlin have denied that.
A second fire was reported at a warehouse containing medicines in Domodedovo, south of Moscow. Analysts identified it as a storage facility the Severnoye Domodedovo logistics center. Ukrainian monitoring channels published numerous videos showing burning warehouses.
Vorobyov said an elderly man was killed after a drone struck a private house in the Ramensky district of the Moscow region. He also reported six people injured.
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyani said three people were injured near the Moscow Ring Road, without specifying the circumstances.
In the southern Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar reported that three people were killed and one was injured in an attack. He did not specify what facility or area had been targeted.
Vorobyov described the attack on the Moscow region as one of the largest in recent times. Sobyanin said around 600 drones had flown toward Moscow since the evening of August 15, with 201 destroyed over the Moscow region.
The Russian Defense Ministry separately reported that 822 drones had been shot down overnight, without specifying how many drones were not intercepted.
The Ukrainian military has not commented on the strikes.
Meanwhile, overnight Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine killed at least one person and injured about 20, Ukrainian officials said.
In Kryviy Rih, an industrial facility was damaged, killing one person and injuring 14 others.
Kyiv reported several fires, including at the Petrovka book market, which was destroyed after catching fire for a second time. Three people were injured in Kyiv and three more in the surrounding Kyiv region. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryviy Rih with missiles and 106 drones.

articles.title: On-the-Lam Polish Politician Surfaces in Renegade, Pro-Moscow Moldova Territory
articles.body:
A senior Polish politician on the run from corruption charges and potentially a quarter-century in prison is living in a breakaway, pro-Moscow region of Moldova outside the reach of Interpol and European justice, news agencies in Moldova and Ukraine reported on Tuesday.
Marcin Romanowski, Poland’s former Deputy Minister of Justice, arrived in Tiraspol, a city on the Danube River in the separatist Moldovan region of Transnistria, via Romania, some reports said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A region predominantly populated by ethnic Russians and Ukrainians, Transnistrian “separatists,” supported by Russian regular military troops based there, gained de fact independence from Moldova in a war fought March-July 1992.
The rebel authorities in the statelet claim they run a self-governing republic loyal to Soviet Marxist tenets. Neither the United Nations nor any major state – including Russia – has recognized Transnistria’s autonomy from Moldova.
According to the Polish radio news platform RMF FM, Romanowski, via lawyers, filed a motion in a Warsaw court, dated Aug. 4, to be granted “safe conduct” in which he promised to return to Poland to face justice including potential trial, provided he is guaranteed free movement as the legal process moved forward. The residential address Romanowski submitted in the motion is in Tiraspol, Moldova, the “capital” of Transnistria.
Poland Proposes European Legion With Ukrainian Veterans
It was the first public document specifying Romanowski’s whereabouts in months. He has been out of Poland and seemingly on the run from justice for more than a year and a half, since a European Arrest Warrant was issued for him on Dec. 19, 2024.
On Tuesday, Polish media citing Romanowski’s attorney Bartosz Lewandowski said investigators had rejected Romanowski’s proposition and that he planned to appeal.
RMF FM, citing Przemysław Nowak, spokesperson for the National Prosecutor’s Office, said that Polish law enforcement considers Lewandowski a significant flight risk because of the potentially severe penalty Lewandowski would face if convicted, and that “above all, the suspect’s hiding from law enforcement agencies abroad for over a year and a half.”
Polish prosecutors have accused Romanowski of illegally manipulating public funds including a fund created to help crime victims while in office, and named 11 acts involving the misappropriation of public funds and abuse of power.
Among other official claims, Romanowski is alleged to have embezzled $27 million in state funds, while also attempting to embezzle an additional $15 million.
He also is alleged to have used Justice Fund money ($6.4 million) to purchase Pegasus software for state use. Critics of the software have claimed Pegasus if operated by a European national government would seriously infringe on individual citizen privacy guarantees.
If convicted of all claimed offenses, he could face up to 25 years in prison under Polish law.
Romanowski has denied the allegations and claimed they are politically motivated. According to Polish news reports, once under the arrest warrant, he first took shelter in a Lublin monastery and later traveled to Hungary without the authorities finding him.
In December 2025, Hungary, at the time run by a pro-Moscow/anti-European government, granted protection to Romanowski from prosecution. In May, Polish media reported Romanowski had left Budapest, following the election of a new Hungarian government supporting Europe and rule of law. Unconfirmed reports since then had placed him in the Balkans.
Moldova, a democratic state with EU aspirations, is not obliged to extradite EU citizens wanted by Interpol, but usually cooperates with European law enforcement agencies thanks to bilateral treaties and agreements.
Transnistria is by comparison an island of relative lawlessness without cooperative agreements with practically any state, except Russia. Under normal circumstances an EU citizen wishing to visit Transnistria enters the region via Moldova receiving an automatic 45-day short-term visa. Extension is possible on a by case basis via Transnistrian authorities.
Reports have not fully confirmed when or how Romanowski entered Transnistrian territory. Romanian law enforcement authorities would, as EU officials, be obliged to seek and, if possible, arrest Romanowski, if he had tried to enter Moldova and Transnistria via Romania.
Ukraine shut down border checkpoints between its territory and lands claimed by Transnistria on Feb. 28, 2022.
Since then, Kyiv has banned civilian traffic across the border. And because there are 1,300 Russian troops still based in Transnistria, the Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) patrol the frontier on a wartime basis.
Romanowski is a serving member of the Polish parliament for the right-wing, nationalist Law and Justice Party. The party supports what it considers “traditional, conservative values” and opposes tight integration between Poland and European law enforcement structures.
The party historically backed strong Polish support of Ukraine against Russia, but since 2023 has actively agitated against Ukraine, accusing Ukrainian grain producers of unfairly competing with Polish farmers, while also accusing Ukrainian refugees in Poland of being a drain on Polish society. The party is dead set against Ukrainian membership in the EU and NATO.
The parasitic refugee accusation is false: According to Polish state data, most of the nearly one million Ukrainian refugees in Poland are gainfully employed and pay taxes. United Nations estimates have put the value of the Ukrainian refugee contribution to the Polish economy between two to three percent of Poland’s GDP.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone in Romania near border with Ukraine
articles.body:
NATO fighter jet shoots down drone in Romania near border with Ukraine
Romania's defense ministry said Sunday a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that had entered its airspace near the border with two of its neighboring countries, Ukraine and Moldova.
The ministry said in a statement the drone had entered from Moldova and was intercepted by a Spanish F-18 jet deployed on NATO duties early Sunday morning. Debris fell in an unpopulated area near the border with Ukraine, the ministry added.
NATO spokesperson Marty O'Donnell said the drone appeared to be Russian. He said it was the fourth successful shootdown of a drone over Romanian airspace by NATO aircraft.
The operation was coordinated through NATO's Combined Air Operations Centre at Torrejón, Spain, O'Donnell said in a statement.
The interception is the latest in a series of similar recurring incidents involving drones straying into Ukraine's neighboring countries' borders, which authorities have blamed on electronic interference as part of the war with Russia. In some cases, the drones are Ukrainian and are "hijacked" by Russian forces.
Authorities have reported finding drone fragments on Romanian soil several times since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River, which lie just across the border. Last week, Ukraine denied targeting Bulgaria after a drone entered the country's airspace on Saturday and exploded close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania.
Last month, Romania shot down a drone for the first time since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after it entered the country's airspace about 60 miles from Bucharest.
In June, Latvia's military said two NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the country's airspace. Ukrainian drones have previously crashed in all three Baltic states, which all share borders with Russia, with officials blaming the inadvertent incursion on Russian electronic warfare.

articles.title: Russians launch ballistic missile strike on industrial facilities in Kryvyi Rih: 2 killed and 14 injured
articles.body:
Russians launch ballistic missile strike on industrial facilities in Kryvyi Rih: 2 killed and 14 injured
Russian forces launched a combined ballistic missile and UAV attack on the city of Kryvyi Rih on the night of 15-16 August. Two people were killed and 14 others were injured.
Source: Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration
Quote: "The enemy struck Kryvyi Rih. Industrial facilities were targeted. A fire broke out. Rescue workers are working at the scene."
Details: At 04:25, Hanzha reported that one person had been killed and six others had been injured in the attack.
According to satellite data from NASA's FIRMS fire and thermal anomaly monitoring service, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine's largest mining and metallurgical company, may have been hit.
Later, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih confirmed that the company had been hit.
Update: In the morning, Hanzha said that the number of people injured had risen to 13.
Quote: "A 48-year-old man has been taken to hospital in a serious condition. Ten people have been taken to hospital in a moderate condition. The other injured people are undergoing examinations."
Update: After 10:00, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration said that rescue workers had recovered another body from under the rubble.
Fourteen more people sustained injuries; of them, 11 were taken to hospital, and a 48-year-old man is in a serious condition.
Background:
- On the night of 15-16 August, Russian forces launched a large-scale attack on several regions of Ukraine using ballistic missiles and attack drones, targeting Kyiv, Kryvyi Rih, Kamianske and Kremenchuk.
- Oleksandr Vilkul, Head of the Kryvyi Rih Defence Council, had reported that the city was under a combined attack involving ballistic missiles and UAVs.
