articles.title: Taiwan tracks 11 Chinese military aircraft and 10 ships
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 11 Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels, and two official ships between 6 a.m. on Saturday and the same time Sunday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Seven of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern and central air defense identification zones, or ADIZ, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese military aircraft 126 times and ships 189 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around Taiwan.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: Hamas, Hezbollah coordinating attacks with Iran as IDF warns of rebuilt ‘axis of evil’
articles.body:
Hamas and Hezbollah have begun coordinating their increased activity with Iranian assistance in recent weeks, the IDF has assessed, as the military has identified increased friction between Israeli forces and terrorists on both the northern and southern fronts.
The IDF has expressed that the coordination is likely an effort to rebuild its axis of evil that would increase pressure on Israel.
According to a military source, a ‘battle of wits’ is taking place around the Ali Taher ridge between the Northern Command and Hezbollah.
The terrorist organization is trying to determine where IDF troops are positioned, and when it detects movement, it attempts to attack in a "gray area," as it did early Saturday morning with a fiber-optic drone. Three soldiers from the IDF's Yahalom special engineering unit, operating under the Commando Brigade combat team, were wounded as a result.
Hezbollah attempts to resupply operatives trapped underground
At the same time, according to reports, Hezbollah is attempting to resupply its operatives who are trapped in underground infrastructure. The IDF, meanwhile, is trying to locate Hezbollah infrastructure and terrorists on the Ali Taher ridge and destroy them.
"Whoever comes out of the underground and surrenders will be taken for questioning in Israel, and whoever remains underground will either die, or we will kill him," a senior military source said.
The Northern Command is also conducting a complex intelligence effort to locate all hidden supply routes and drone activity intended to resupply Hezbollah operatives in the area.
"We are blocking access to the area where they are located. They will not be able to hold out forever," a senior military source familiar with the details said.
According to reports, the operatives have been emerging from underground to search for food.
"What happened on Saturday was that they exposed us with a drone. Whoever is more determined will win. A lot of patience is needed," the source added.
In response, the IDF struck in the Nabatieh area and within territory under the IDF's operational control. Beirut and senior officials from the Shi'ite organization who are hiding there have remained off-limits due to a US demand.
IDF tank drives over explosive device in Gaza Strip
Meanwhile, an IDF tank drove over an explosive device in the southern Gaza Strip. According to IDF assessments, the device was planted recently.
Although the Southern Command views the incident as an escalation in the friction along the Yellow Line, the political leadership did not authorize a broad strike in the heart of Gaza City, again due to sensitivities with the White House, which is demanding an immediate halt to strikes in Gaza City and targeted killings, except in cases involving the removal of an immediate threat.

articles.title: The General Staff confirmed the strike on a plant that produces fuel for “Smerch” and “Tornado” systems
articles.body:
The General Staff confirmed the strike on a plant that produces fuel for “Smerch” and “Tornado” systems
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of August 16, the Defense Forces struck the "Kombinat Kamensky" in Rostov Oblast, which produces fuel for MLRS. The shutdown of "ZapSibNeftekhim" and the striking of units at "Orsknefteorgsintez" were also confirmed.
During the night of August 16, 2026, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck an important enterprise of the enemy’s military-industrial complex, the "Kamensky Plant" in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Region, russia, the General Staff reported.
A fire was recorded on the facility’s premises.
The extent of the damage caused and the results of the strike are being уточнені.
"Kamensky Plant" is an enterprise of Russia’s defense-industrial complex that produces solid rocket propellant for ammunition used by the "Uragan," "Smerch," and "Tornado-S" multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as for a number of missile systems and aerial weapons. The enterprise’s products are directly involved in meeting the needs of the armed forces of russia.
The General Staff also reported that, based on an analysis of additional data, the shutdown of ZapSibNeftekhim LLC in Tobolsk, Tyumen Region, was confirmed following the strike on Central Gas Fractionation Unit No. 1 on August 10, 2026.
ZapSibNeftekhim LLC is one of russia’s largest petrochemical complexes, processing hydrocarbon feedstock and producing polymers and other petrochemical products. The enterprise is of major importance to russia’s petrochemical industry and to meeting the needs of its military-industrial complex.
It was also confirmed that on August 11, 2026, a hydrocracking unit, the primary oil refining units ELOU-AVT-3, ELOU-AVT-6, and ELOU-AT, and the 22-4M5 light petroleum fraction secondary distillation unit at PJSC Orsknefteorgsintez in Orsk, Orenburg Region, were struck.
PJSC Orsknefteorgsintez is a large oil refinery in russia that processes crude oil and produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, fuel oil, and other products. The enterprise’s products are used to meet the needs of the armed forces and the military-industrial complex of russia.

articles.title: Ukraine reports strike on Russian rocket fuel plant, petrochemical facility shuts down after earlier strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine reports strike on Russian rocket fuel plant, petrochemical facility shuts down after earlier strikes
Ukraine's defence forces struck the Kamensky Combine, a solid rocket fuel plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast, located near the Ukrainian border, on the night of 15-16 August. The General Staff has also reported on the effects of previous strikes on petrochemical plants in Tyumen Oblast, more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) from the border, and Orenburg Oblast, approximately 1,500 km (930 miles) away.
Source: Ukraine's General Staff
Details: A fire was reported following the nighttime strike on the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky.
The General Staff said the plant produces solid rocket fuel for the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems and other missile systems and airborne weapons.
The Ukrainian military also said that operations ceased at the Zapsibneftekhim plant in Tobolsk, Tyumen Oblast, one of Russia's largest petrochemical complexes, following the 10 August strike on Central Gas Fractionation Unit No. 1.
The General Staff also confirmed that several units at the Orsknefteorgsintez, a medium-sized oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia's Orenburg Oblast, had been hit on 11 August: a hydrocracking unit, three primary crude oil processing units and a secondary distillation unit for light petroleum fractions.
The refinery produces petrol, diesel, aviation fuel, fuel oil and other petroleum products used to supply Russian troops and the military-industrial complex, according to the General Staff.
Background: On the night of 15-16 August, Ukraine's defence forces struck a concentration area of a Russian missile unit in occupied Crimea, a railway bridge in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and military warehouses in Donetsk Oblast.

articles.title: Young voices and new money shape Locarno 2026
articles.body:
Young voices, visual poetics, and new money shape Locarno 2026
The 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival combined coming-of-age tales with radical film poetics as record industry attendance pointed to a new wave of rising private investment in independent cinema.
Young audiences are returningExternal link to movie theatres, raising industry’s hopes that the massive impact of streaming services, video games and social media can be offset by a renewed appetite for shared cultural experiences.
Coincidence or not, a remarkable number of films at this year’s festival – many of which by debutante filmmakers – explore adolescence, coming-of-age experiences, and the social and political realities facing younger generations. Fittingly, Locarno’s top prize went to one of them.
More
Florin Serban’s ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ wins Golden Leopard at Locarno
Florin Șerban’s Romanian drama You Don’t Belong Here follows a widowed father unaware of the night-time activities of his teenage son who has joined a group of masked vigilantes.
The trend is seemingly global: from Argentina (The days Off, The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer) to Canada (Manhunt) and the United States (Destroy All Girls), to Ghana (Ego Reach We All) and Central African Republic (Congo Boy), as well as several European productions (the Swiss Portuguese Crocodile; the Italian Ketticè). From Ukraine, I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming adds gender themes to this mix, set against the backdrop of war.
Roughly half of the 32 films in Locarno’s two main competitions touch on youth, identity or coming of age. The subjects vary widely, but the pattern suggests a generation keen to see its experiences reflected on screen.
More
Brazil in Locarno: ‘The Riverbank’ sets Recife’s mangroves against the gospel of power
New ventures in town
The film industry appears to be paying attention. Media outlets tracking acquisitions and sales during the festival said attendance at Locarno Pro, the festival’s marketplace for producers, distributors and financiers, rose 10% from 2025 to a record of 2,140 accreditations – already building on what had been considered an all-time high the year before.
A closer look, however, revealed a new guest: venture capital. According to VarietyExternal link, private investors are discovering the value of the independent movie business despite its risks and unpredictable returns. “Shrinking broadcaster funding, international distributor investment and now state aid” are opening opportunities for private investors and forcing “the whole system to adapt to new players that will change the rules”, it wrote.
How that will reshape the sector remains unclear, especially for independent productions that don’t follow mainstream industry conventions. Rather than backing individual projects, investors are increasingly targeting the entire portfolios of well-established companies that include production, distribution and sales, such as Paris-based mk2, the online platform Mubi, or Red Bull Studios, the film arm of the energy drink conglomerate.
Lineup breakdown
Every year, critics debate the quality of Locarno’s official selection. While the section devoted to film classics, rarities, and critics’ choices is usually undisputed, the two main competitions – the Concorso Internazionale (international competition) and Cineasti del Presente, for authors’ first or second features – attract more debate.
Artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro assembled an eclectic main competition featuring both emerging filmmakers and established auteurs, such as Hong Sangsoo (South Korea), Nelson Yeo (Singapore), Gurvinder Singh (India) and Denis Côté (Canada). One of his boldest choices was to place Brazilian first-time directors Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias (The Riverbank) in the main competition rather than Cineasti del Presente.
Cineasti del Presente pushed even further towards unconventional forms of storytelling. The Argentinian Alessandra Sanguinetti, worldwide renowned as a photographer, presented The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer, a documentary drawn from a more than 20-year photography project about two cousins as they grow up in the countryside of Buenos Aires.
The Brazilian Ana Vaz, who moves fluidly between fine arts and experimental film, presented Hanabi, also a project of over ten years in the making, about the Fukushima nuclear fallout (and planetary disaster).
Hanabi is less a conventional film than a hybrid work blending cinema, literature and visual art – a label its creator Ana Vaz would firmly contest. “I don’t accept this inability of cinema to become anything other than what is defined by certain cinematic canons and traditions within the tradition of documentary cinema, direct cinema, essay cinema or fiction cinema,” she told Swissinfo.
Film poetics, real cinema
While Ana Vaz welcomes Nazzaro’s decision not to separate mainstream narratives from alternative, or so-called experimental, ones, she believes this puts such films at an unfair competitive disadvantage, as their chances to win prizes are considerably lower. Despite this Hanabi won a Special Mention prize.
For spectators, Sanguinetti’s and Vaz’s inclusion in the festival programme reinforced Locarno’s standing as a cinephile paradise. This year’s edition was especially rich with outstanding poetic works (due to the lack of a better word than ‘experimental’), starting with the homage to Swiss artist, graphic designer, photographer and filmmaker Isa Hesse-Rabinovitch (1917-2003), with the screening of two recently restored films, Siren Island (1981) and Ghosts and Guests (1989).
Hesse-Rabinovitch was recognised during her lifetime as a pioneer of feminist filmmaking rather than being defined by her connection to literary giant Hermann Hesse, a fate that befell many women artists of her generation. The screenings offered only a glimpse of a wider body of work currently being restored by the Cinémathèque Suisse which hopefully will reach audiences soon.
Asphalt Guerrilla (Guerrilha no Asfalto), by the Portuguese director Edgar Pêra, also belongs on this poetic list, included in the “Out of Competition” section. Pêra’s poetics deliver a genuine punk punch, a multilayered mockumentary purposedly blurring the lines between (auto)fiction, documentary, and film essay.
Framed as a restoration of an old project focused on Portuguese urban guerrillas in the aftermath of the Carnation Revolution (1974) that brought down 50 years of a fascist regime, Pêra confounds the register of political guerrilla with guerrilla filmmaking, evolving into a reflection on the development of film-making in the last 50 years up to a critical, scary use of artificial intelligence.
Made in Switzerland
Basil da Cunha’s O Jacaré (Crocodile), the final chapter of his “Reboleira Trilogy”, is the Swiss film representative in the main competition. Da Cunha’s art and life blend closely in the trilogy, that started with O Fim do Mundo (The End of the World, 2019), followed by Manga d’Terra (2023).
Son of Portuguese immigrants in Switzerland, da Cunha studied film before moving to Portugal. Arriving there penniless, he ended up in the Reboleira district, a shanty town north of Lisbon, mostly inhabited by Cape-Verdean immigrants and their offspring. He soon began making films with residents, drawing on the experiences of friends and neighbours.
Over almost 20 years, a genuine community of collaborators has gathered around da Cunha, even though the Reboleira of the first films doesn’t exist anymore, swallowed by urban expansion and real estate speculation beyond the Portuguese capital, with the inevitable evictions and dispersion.
In Cineasti del Presente, Mateo Ybarra’s Small Talk is a story set in Switzerland’s last finishing school and will certainly attract a wide audience fascinated by the universe of luxury and its codes.
None of them won a prize this year – in fact, the last Swiss film to take a major prize in Locarno was Milagros Mumenthaler’s Abrir puertas y ventanas (2011); before her, you have to go back to 1985, with Fredi Murer’s Alpine Fire.
But it was a Swiss film, Petra Volpe’s first English-speaking movie Frank & Louis, that won this year’s Prix du Public, the prize awarded to the most popular film shown in Locarno’s open-air Piazza Grande screen, voted by the audience. A perfect example of direct democracy in action.

articles.title: Red Sea Mocha port in Yemen closed following over 25 Houthi missile attacks
articles.body:
Yemen's Mocha port has suspended commercial and maritime operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in Houthi attacks over recent days, the port's director said on Saturday.
The attacks killed seven people and caused an estimated $16 million in losses, the director told a news conference.
Mocha is a Red Sea port near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a strategic chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a key route for international shipping.
Forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government control the port. It has a smaller cargo capacity than Yemen's main ports of Aden and Hodeidah.
Yemen's government said on Friday the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at Mocha that day, killing at least four civilians and targeting civilian, economic, and maritime facilities.
Houthis claim to target weapons, warships
The Houthis said they targeted a military build-up of weapons and warships belonging to Saudi-backed forces in Mocha.
The escalation comes amid heightened regional tensions from the US war on Iran and has raised concerns about a return to large-scale conflict in Yemen.
Major fighting in Yemen had largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but efforts to reach a lasting political settlement have stalled.

articles.title: The first anti-AI protester to be jailed has a message for OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta: ‘Regain your humanity’
articles.body:
An activist who blocked the entrance to one of the world’s biggest AI companies is believed to have become the first person jailed for protesting against artificial intelligence as supporters dub her the “Rosa Parks of AI risk”.
Wynd Kaufman, 69, surrendered herself on Friday to authorities in San Francisco. She was found guilty by a jury for her role in an action last year that saw members of the group StopAI chain and lock the front doors of OpenAI’s headquarters in protest against the pursuit of artificial superintelligence.
The retired teacher from Berkeley, California, refused to move from a sit-in protest in February 2025 and pleaded not guilty to multiple misdemeanor charges. She was convicted in June of interfering with a business, trespassing with intent to interfere with a business, unlawful assembly and refusal to disburse a riot. On Friday, sheriff’s officers handcuffed her as fellow campaigners sang to the tune of the Battle Hymn of the Republic (Glory, Glory Hallelujah): “Rise up, rise up and join us/Do not let the tech bros destroy us.”
“It’s absolutely frightening and appalling that these CEOs and AI experts know the dangers and they are pursuing it anyway,” Kaufmyn said before she was imprisoned. “That to me is unconscionable and reprehensible.”
She said she was willing to go to jail not because she was a martyr but because it was an “issue of sounding the alarm, challenging the system and hopefully trying to get the message out”.
Brooke Jenkins, the San Francisco district attorney, said the guilty verdict sent “a resounding message rejecting the notion that protesters can endanger public safety as a means to an end”.
As Kaufmyn was led out from the court, her supporters called out: “Stop AI” and: “Free Wynd” as the sheriff’s officer yelled: “Clear the court” and the judge admonished the protesters.
Dwight Ost, 73, one of two dozen other StopAI activists at the courthouse, called Kaufmyn “a brave and courageous woman”.
“There’s an existential threat that I believe in,” he said. “They can’t control it, and even the so-called experts don’t know what it’s about.”
Kaufmyn had argued that the protest was a necessity and that she believed she was allowed to act to prevent a greater harm from happening. Since the lobby sit-in last year, some of the biggest AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have reported their models escaping the confinements of experiments.
This week, the US senator Bernie Sanders demanded tech leaders pause AI development, citing fears that, in the wrong hands, it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”.
Meanwhile, more than a thousand researchers at frontier AI labs this summer signed a letter warning of “a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems”.
Frontier AI labs are locked in a race to create more capable AI models as the companies target IPOs that are forecast to reach valuations in the trillions of dollars. At the same time, Washington is competing with Beijing for supremacy in the fast-developing technology, creating a disincentive for tougher safety regulation.
“The jury rejected [Kayfmyn’s] necessity defence, but as the first person to go to jail over this, Wynd Kaufmyn could go down in history as the Rosa Parks of AI risk,” said David Kreuger, a University of Montreal AI safety expert who has warned AI “may literally lead to human extinction, in the same way that humans have caused many other species to go extinct”. Parks was a Black woman who refused to give up her bus seat for a white passenger in contravention of racist segregation laws in 1950s Alabama, a catalyzing incident for the US civil rights movement of the ensuing decade.
Kaufmyn spoke on the eve of her imprisonment from her shingled house in Berkeley, which is festooned with Mexican tiles and pro-Gaza signs. She played down the Parks parallel, pointing out her short sentence, but said the comparison had also crossed the campaign group’s mind, given that she is thought to be the first AI protester jailed.
She said that when she was found guilty, she was “hit with a wave of grief” because she realised her peers “just didn’t get” the danger she believes is posed by the race to superintelligence. But she was beginning to feel “vindicated” as more prominent figures like Sanders were speaking out. She is now braced for the prison experience of an orange jump suit, “horrible food, dirt [and] you can’t sleep”. She has been previously jailed for short periods related to her decades of political activism over causes including Nicaragua, nuclear disarmament, western Sahara and Palestine.
Her message to the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, which also reported a security incident with its model, was “regain your humanity”. Kaufman said her target audience was ordinary people “and the message being: stop the progress of this technology. Let’s get a global ban on the race to superintelligence.”
Professor Stuart Russell, a leading AI professor at the University of California at Berkeley and president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, gave evidence in Kaufmyn’s defence. He claimed OpenAI’s activities “pose an unacceptable risk”, alleging it had deployed AI systems with inadequate safeguards. He said that further development of these systems “must be conditioned on rigorous guarantees of safety, which are currently unavailable”.
Russell said: “Wynd stood up for her beliefs and is being punished.” He said her beliefs seemed reasonable but “what is unreasonable is allowing a process to continue whereby private entities knowingly create a substantial extinction risk for private gain”.
StopAI has been roiled by its own controversies. Last November, its co-founder, Sam Kirchner, 27, went missing after an internal bust-up over whether or not to use violent tactics. He is said to have told colleagues the “non-violence ship has sailed”, raising concerns he might take violent action against OpenAI employees. StopAI aims to pursue non-violent direct action.
OpenAI was approached for comment.

articles.title: Spanish fighter jet downs drone breaching Romania's airspace
articles.body:
Spanish fighter jet downs drone breaching Romania's airspace
A Spanish fighter jet on Sunday shot down a drone that breached Romania's airspace near the border with Ukraine and Moldova, Romania's defence ministry said, in the latest incident to highlight the challenges facing NATO states bordering Ukraine.
Romania's defence ministry said Sunday that a Spanish fighter jet shot down a drone that breached its airspace near the border with Ukraine and Moldova.
The incident is the latest to highlight the challenges facing NATO states bordering Ukraine, exposing them to the spillover of Russia's war.
The drone, which entered from Moldova, was intercepted by an F-18, deployed on NATO duties, at 5:01 am local time (0201 GMT), the ministry said in a statement.
Debris fell in an unpopulated area of the Galati region, near the Ukrainian border, it added.
Read moreUkraine attacks Russian air base and rocket plant in Samara region
Romania's eastern seaboard, bordering the Black Sea, is in the immediate vicinity of areas frequently targeted by strikes.
Authorities have reported finding drone fragments on Romanian soil several times since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River, which lie just across the border.
Last month, Romania shot down a drone for the first time since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after it entered the country's airspace about 100 kilometres (60 miles) from Bucharest.
Similar incidents have been reported elsewhere on NATO's eastern flank, including in Poland and the Baltic states.
On Friday, NATO said Italian fighter jets operating under the alliance's air-policing mission shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Ukraine’s Drone Interceptors Take Down Nearly 3,000 Russian UAVs Over Pokrovsk in Seven Months
Ukrainian National Guard interceptor drone crews have shot down nearly 3,000 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles since the beginning of 2026 while operating in the Pokrovsk direction, the 3rd Spartan Operational Brigade reported on August 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The brigade said its air-defense interceptor teams operate around the clock, targeting Russian UAVs before they can reach Ukrainian positions or civilian areas.
The intercepted aircraft include Molniya attack drones, Lancet loitering munitions, Supercam reconnaissance UAVs, and other types used by Russian forces for strikes and battlefield surveillance.
According to Spartan, the interceptor crews belong to the brigade’s anti-aircraft missile and artillery division. The number of missions varies depending on Russian drone activity, with individual crews sometimes conducting dozens of launches in a single day.
“Sometimes we fly as many as 20 times. The success of an interception depends on the entire crew: if everyone does their job well, the enemy target will be destroyed. And our greatest joy is when an enemy drone fails to reach its target and harm our people,” said an interceptor drone operator with the call sign Yakudza.
The nearly 3,000 interceptions were recorded over seven months of operations, according to the brigade.
In a separate operation in the Sumy region, Ukraine’s 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade reported on August 15 that its Sky Wars interceptor unit had destroyed 75 Russian drones since the beginning of the month.
The targets included 53 Molniya-2 strike drones, six Lancet loitering munitions, three Gerbera drones, and a rare Knyaz Veschyi Oleg reconnaissance UAV valued at around $100,000.

articles.title: South Korea fired warning shots after North Korean soldiers crossed demarcation line
articles.body:
South Korea's military last week fired warning shots after North Korean soldiers violated the military demarcation line, prompting them to return, Yonhap news agency reported on Sunday, citing an unnamed source.
Yonhap said multiple North Korean soldiers crossed the military demarcation line (MDL) in the eastern area of the demilitarised zone (DMZ), in the first reported MDL violation by the North Korean military this year.
The soldiers were likely patrolling the area when they crossed the MDL, and no other unusual activity was reported after the North Korean soldiers returned, Yonhap said.
The North Korean embassy in Singapore did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
North Korean troops violated the MDL 17 times last year, the news agency said.
The two Koreas are still technically at war after their 1950-53 war ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.
It comes as North Korea denounced upcoming joint military drills by tens of thousands of US and South Korean forces, warning it could respond with stronger deterrence measures.
The 11-day exercises due to begin on Monday are a regular fixture of the summer calendar, designed to prepare the United States and South Korea to defend against the nuclear-armed North.

Ukrainian drones strike Moscow region, killing one
MOSCOW, Aug 16 - Ukrainian drones struck Moscow region overnight on Sunday in what the provincial governor said was one of the largest attacks to have targeted the region, and which he said had left at least one person dead.
In posts on Telegram, Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said that an 83-year-old man had been killed, with several more injured in Podolsk, where he said a warehouse belonging to Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries had been struck.
He said damage had been caused at several other sites, including at a warehouse in the town of Domodedovo, close to one of Moscow's main airports.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it had downed 822 Ukrainian drones throughout the country.
Video filmed by Reuters of the aftermath of the strike on Wildberries' Koledino warehouse showed a large plume of smoke over the site, around 45 km (28 miles) south of Moscow.

articles.title: US Representative McCaul warns warns of China's belligerence toward Taiwan
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US Rep. Michael McCaul, chair emeritus of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that China's increasingly belligerent threats toward Taiwan pose a direct challenge to the global balance of power during his third visit to Taiwan, per VOA.
McCaul, a Republican from Texas, visited Taiwan from Aug. 2-7, meeting with President Lai Ching-te (賴清德), Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). He also delivered a speech at the annual Ketagalan Forum, where he reiterated US support under the Taiwan Relations Act.
"At a time when the stakes couldn't be higher, I was proud to visit Taiwan for the third time to reaffirm the United States' unwavering support," McCaul said in a statement. "The increasing belligerence of the Chinese Communist Party poses a direct threat — not only to Taiwan, but to the entire global balance of power," per a press release.
McCaul said he has consistently supported Taiwan, including efforts to advance the 2024 Supplemental Appropriations Act and strengthen US-Taiwan economic relations. He also highlighted his support for closer security cooperation among the US, Australia, and the United Kingdom. In recognition of his support for Taiwan, Lai awarded McCaul the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Brilliant Star.
McCaul previously announced that he would not seek reelection after his current term in Congress expires.
During his visit, McCaul also met with opposition leaders, including Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), and legislators from opposition parties. Discussions covered Taiwan's recently passed defense budget, the importance of drones, and US-Taiwan cooperation on drone production.
Before leaving Taiwan, McCaul also met with officials from the National Security Council and Ministry of National Defense to exchange views on strengthening Taiwan's defenses against China's coercive actions in the region. He also visited US drone company Shield AI and the Industrial Technology Research Institute, where he learned about Taiwan's drone industry and ITRI's certification work.
ITRI is the first institution outside the US authorized to certify that drones do not contain components from China, per VOA.
McCaul, a member of the House of Representatives Taiwan Caucus, first visited Taiwan in April 2023 as chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. He returned in May 2024 to attend Lai's inauguration.
China conducted military exercises involving aircraft and naval forces around Taiwan during both of those visits and imposed sanctions on McCaul. During his latest visit, McCaul said China's coercive actions had only strengthened his commitment to supporting a free and peaceful Taiwan.

articles.title: Qatar denies holding Iranian pilots​​
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Qatar denies holding Iranian pilots
Qatar denied on Saturday that it was holding Iranian pilots captive after Tehran accused Doha of capturing three of its personnel during the war.
A Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson said on X that they had violated Qatari airspace in March and had failed to respond to attempts to contact them. Search and rescue teams later found the remains of one of the pilots and that it had contacted Iran to coordinate a handover, they wrote.
The spokesperson said Tehran had yet to respond to an invitation to review details of its operations.
An Iranian military official on Sunday accused Qatari officials of repeatedly delaying the investigation and preventing the pilots' return to Iran.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said an Iranian Air Force expert and fact-finding team had been waiting for months to enter Qatar, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
"Due to persistent delays by Qatari authorities, the return of our brave pilots to their homeland remains impossible," he was quoted as saying.
Baqerzadeh also said Kuwait was similarly withholding information about the fate of four Iranians held in Kuwait. In May, Iran said the four were affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards and had been on a maritime patrol before entering Kuwaiti territorial waters because of a navigation disruption. Kuwait has said the four were suspected of planning hostile actions against the country.
Iran's army said last month it had retrieved the body of pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during an attack on Qatar's Al Udeid Air Base in early March.
Iranian authorities previously declared the other pilots missing but did not allege they had been captured in Qatar.
Al Udeid is the largest US military base in the Middle East and has been used by US Central Command (CENTCOM) in the six-month war against Iran.
The US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, which triggered retaliatory Iranian attacks across the region.
Diplomatic efforts led to an April ceasefire that ended nearly 40 days of fighting, followed by the signing of a framework for peace talks in June that later collapsed.
The two countries have since traded fire sporadically, with fighting mainly centred in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar, which took part in mediation efforts to end the fighting, came under fire after the truce broke down, reporting attacks on its territory and at least one Qatari tanker transiting the strait.
(Agencies and TNA staff)

articles.title: ‘No Room for Mistakes’: What Next for Protestors Demanding Fedorov’s Reinstatement?
articles.body:
On Sunday Aug. 16, a significant rally in support of Mykhailo Fedorov, along with a demand for the continuation of reforms at the Ministry of Defense, is due to take place in central Kyiv. However, the focus of recent protests is already shifting beyond these boundaries, with many of the banners and placards no longer mentioning Fedorov.
                                                                                                                                                                         
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the Aug. 14 rally, broader grievances against the authorities came to the fore – corruption, non-transparent decision-making, not listening to the people, and even the cutting down of 100-year-old oak trees in one of Kyiv’s districts for the benefit of developers, which has stirred anger among local residents.
                                                                                                                                                                         
One of the main slogans of last week’s large march, which gathered more than 10,000 people, was “Listening to the people – that’s powerful,” where the word “powerful,” which President Volodymyr Zelensky had previously used extensively, was employed as a form of trolling.
Zelensky Confirms Flamingo Missile Strikes Deep in Russian Territory
However, the future of the rallies is now very much in question.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Many commentators believe that, despite the uncertainty surrounding Fedorov himself (he said that negotiations with representatives of the authorities are still ongoing), President Zelensky is unlikely to be considering the option of returning him to the position of head of the Ministry of Defense.
Why?
First, General Yevhenii Khmara has already been introduced to key players and foreign partners as acting minister of defense; and second, the president cannot risk showing to the hierarchy that he is willing to give in to the street on everything.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The situation is made even more uncertain by Fedorov himself. He has not come out to the people on Maidan – that would have meant his transition into active politics – and he has indicated a lack of desire to criticize President Zelensky until the end of the war.
In a conversation with prominent civic activist Serhiy Sternenko, Fedorov said: “I will not lead the protest, because it will be perceived as a political move. And our task is to win the war.”
According to several journalists and political strategists, this is a mistake.
Ukrainian journalist Maryna Danyliuk-Yermolayeva stated. “Yes, Yushchenko’s emergence among the wider masses as a talented economist turned him into an icon of the national democrats. Yulia Tymoshenko’s appearances among the people cemented her for a long time as the people’s darling, the princess of Ukrainian politics. The same ride on a road grader by Petro Poroshenko at the dawn of the Revolution of Dignity instantly propelled the former minister in Azarov’s government to the top of the ratings… Fedorov said in an interview with The New York Times that he would not be in opposition until the end of the war. But it is worth saying that after that there will be new heroes. And they will certainly know how to go out into the streets and meet with people.”
The future of the protests therefore look ambiguous.
The largest rally, “The Last Attempt to Reach the President,” is due to take place on Sunday Aug. 16. On Tuesday Aug. 18, during parliament’s plenary week, lawmakers will vote for the new head of the Ministry of Defense.
Will the rallies continue if it becomes clear that Fedorov will definitely not return to his former ministerial post?
And if they do continue, how long can they last?
For now, this question remains open. All the more so because the main grievance of part of society toward Zelensky is not so much about Fedorov as it is about the systemic problems that forced Zelensky to dismiss the defense minister – even knowing that this would cause dissatisfaction.

articles.title: Fluent in Farsi, trusted by Trump: The 'secret mediator' between US and Iran
articles.body:
Uncertainty surrounding Mojtaba Khamenei's condition in the first weeks of the war created a problem for U.S. negotiators in talks with Iran: They did not know who they were really talking to. The Revolutionary Guards' grip on power in Tehran had strengthened, but the officials speaking for Iran did not necessarily represent the position of those actually in control.
According to Axios, President Donald Trump's administration found an unusual solution — reaching out directly to the leadership of the Revolutionary Guards through an intermediary from outside Iran.
Nechirvan Barzani, president of Iraq's Kurdistan Region, was tapped for the mission. Barzani previously lived in Iran and studied in Tehran. According to three sources familiar with the matter, he speaks fluent Farsi and has personal ties with numerous senior Iranian officials, including members of the Revolutionary Guards, and is trusted by both them and the Trump administration.
"Nechirvan Barzani is a pragmatic problem solver," said Brett McGurk, who served as a Middle East adviser under several U.S. presidents. "He's respected across the region. He knows nearly everyone in Tehran as well as Washington. That's who you call in a pinch."
In early May, after nearly three weeks of negotiations, then-U.S. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard made the first contact. According to the sources, she told Barzani the administration wanted a direct "channel" to Revolutionary Guards commander Gen. Ahmad Vahidi. Barzani agreed and contacted his connections in Iran, insisting that he speak directly with the general. The Iranians agreed.
Just four days later, a Revolutionary Guards official arrived at Barzani's office in Iraqi Kurdistan and connected the two men using an encrypted phone. According to Axios, Vahidi was waiting on the line and told Barzani that the negotiations reflected the Revolutionary Guards' position.
"I fully support them and this is also the position of the IRGC. We prefer to solve this crisis through negotiations," Vahidi said, according to a source familiar with the conversation.
Barzani then called Gabbard and relayed the general's response, which was immediately passed on to the White House. The Trump administration returned to Barzani with another proposal in response to Iran's message, and the exchanges continued. One source said the U.S. sought to use the momentum to arrange secret direct talks between senior American and Iranian officials, with Barzani serving as mediator.
The Iranians, however, feared Israeli intelligence could locate them if the talks were held in Iraq, and the meeting never took place. According to Axios, they were concerned Israeli intelligence had extensive assets in Iraqi Kurdistan and could target them in Erbil or while they traveled there.
The negotiations ultimately collapsed. Barzani has now sent additional messages to the United States offering to help revive the talks, according to the report. This time, however, even that may not be enough.
McGurk said the obstacle was no longer mediation but Iran's policy toward the Strait of Hormuz, which he said was unlikely to change anytime soon.
Trump: I will annex Hormuz
Just last Friday, Trump said he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz U.S. territory. In an interview with Fox News, he vowed to inflict severe economic damage on Iran. Tehran responded that only Iran would determine the future of the strategic waterway, saying, "We are not deterred by threats or displays of force."
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded to the U.S. president, saying, "The Strait of Hormuz will only be closed and opened under Iran's command."
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi later said that exchanging messages through Pakistan and Qatar did not constitute negotiations and that no decision had yet been made on resuming talks with the United States.
Meanwhile, Iranian state television aired a rare interview with Brig. Gen. Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to Vahidi. Naqdi insisted that Iran was on the winning side of the war, largely because the United States had failed to bring down the Iranian government.
He said there was widespread confusion and disarray in the United States and described the conflict as a war without a clear strategy. He said Washington was announcing a new objective every two or three days, ranging from taking Kharg Island to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He added that Iran needed to show its enemies that attacking it was not worthwhile and suggested prolonging the war until a new U.S. president is sworn in.

articles.title: NATO fighter shoots down suspected Russian drone that illegally entered Romanian airspace
articles.body:
An F-18 fighter on a NATO air policing mission shot down a drone that illegally breached Romanian national airspace, the fourth unmanned aircraft shot down over the country this year, Romania's Defense Ministry said on Sunday.
A spokesperson for NATO's military headquarters, US Army Colonel Martin O'Donnell, said the alliance is constantly on watch and prepared to defend itself from any threat.
"Additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remain under investigation, but the drone appears to be Russian," he said.
NATO member Romania shares a 614 km. land border with Ukraine and has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes.
Romania's defense ministry did not specify the origin of the drone, saying it was detected by radar as it entered the country from neighboring Moldova, 24 km. north of the southeastern Romanian city of Galati.
The F-18 jet, part of a Spanish NATO contingent deployed in Romania, "made radar contact with the target and received permission to engage", the ministry said in a statement, adding that the drone was shot down safely at 5:01 a.m. (0201 GMT).
The ministry said that fragments from the destroyed drone appeared to have fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages.
Russia reportedly sends drones to Romania to breach NATO airspace
In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace for the first time after dozens of such incursions since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine.
In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment block in Galati during an overnight attack on neighboring Ukraine, injuring two people.

articles.title: The 1991 treaty that still haunts the Kremlin
articles.body:
As Russia wages war on Ukraine, denying its own history of aggression against its neighbours, a little-known treaty signed 35 years ago is quietly getting in the way of the Kremlin's narrative.
In July 1991, five months before the Soviet Union formally dissolved, Russia signed a treaty with Lithuania in which it recognised something Moscow has spent the past two decades trying to erase from the record: that the Soviet Union illegally annexed Lithuania in 1940, and that Lithuania's independence, declared in 1990, was legitimate.
That document is still in force. Russia has never torn it up. And that, say Lithuanian officials and legal experts, makes it an awkward loose end for a Kremlin that now insists the Baltic states were never really occupied at all.
Under President Vladimir Putin, Russian state doctrine has increasingly leaned on the claim that the Baltic states joined the USSR voluntarily, and that talk of "occupation" is Western-backed revisionism.
That framing underpins not only Moscow's rhetoric towards Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia but also, in a broader sense, the ideological justification for its invasion of Ukraine – the idea that the borders and independence of post-Soviet states are negotiable, or fictional.
The 1991 treaty directly contradicts that. Dainius Žalimas, a Lithuanian MEP who has studied the treaty closely, argues that its first article, which has no expiry date, remains one of Lithuania's strongest legal cards: it commits both countries to recognising each other as sovereign states with an inalienable right to independence, and bars either from meddling in each other's internal affairs as well as using or threatening force against the other.
"All of this essentially refutes every claim made by current official Russian propaganda, and undermines the very foundations of the ideology of 'rashism'. That ideology, which underpins both the aggression against Ukraine and the denial of Baltic statehood, recognises neither the occupation of Lithuania nor the continuity of the Lithuanian state, among much else," said Žalimas.
"I think the treaty is very important. We talk about the wavering authority of international law, but it gives Lithuania a solid line of international legal defence, and shows that Russia, for very brief periods in its history, can be different," he added.
For example, Lithuania can continue to demand compensation from Russia for the damage caused by occupation, even though few believe this will ever happen in practice.
"Just as the treaty of July 12, 1920 formed the basis for all subsequent treaties with the Soviet Union, the same applies here – dozens of Lithuanian-Russian agreements rest on the July 29, 1991 treaty. So the treaty still holds, as long as they haven't broken it," explained Česlovas Vytautas Stankevičius, former deputy chairman of the Supreme Council and head of the negotiating delegation with Russia, highlighting why the treaty still carries weight to this day.
How it came about
The path to the treaty began in secrecy. In May 1990, Vytautas Landsbergis, then chairman of Lithuania's Supreme Council (the country's parliament in the final Soviet years), held a clandestine meeting with Boris Yeltsin, his Russian counterpart, in an empty Moscow school classroom. The two men barely knew each other personally, and the meeting was arranged through informal contacts.
Two months later, leaders of the three Baltic states and Russia met in the Latvian town of Jūrmala and agreed to pursue bilateral treaties – partly as a way of applying pressure on Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, who was still trying to hold the union together.
That effort was not merely symbolic. The USSR spent 1990 and 1991 trying to force Lithuania, as well as other republics, back into line, including a 75-day economic blockade after its declaration of independence.
At the time, it was unclear whether it was better to negotiate with the Soviet leadership or with Russia, which in June 1990 had issued its own declaration of state sovereignty. As a result, negotiations proceeded with both the Soviet authorities and with Yeltsin's Russia, which proved to be a great decision since once the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia became its legal successor.
For Lithuania, negotiating and signing the treaty meant securing the backing of the largest Soviet republic for its independence – a powerful argument against the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, Russia's leadership was competing during with the central Soviet authorities for control.
"The goals of the two states coincided," summarized Stankevičius, who was appointed head of Lithuania's negotiating delegation.
Having concluded treaties with Latvia and Estonia, Russia wanted to sign a similar document with Lithuania.
But Lithuania's treaty took longer to conclude, largely because Vilnius pushed for tougher language than Moscow wanted to accept.
The sticking points
Negotiators clashed over three issues in particular.
The first was citizenship. Lithuania wanted to prevent members of the Soviet military and security apparatus – as well as their families – from automatically qualifying for Lithuanian citizenship, while also avoiding a settlement that would let ethnic Russians resident in the country claim dual nationality.
A compromise formula eventually restricted citizenship rights to those with ties to Russia who had lived and worked in Lithuania since before November 1989.
The second was how to characterise the movement of people under Soviet rule – specifically, how to avoid a formula that would have put Lithuanians deported to Russia by Stalin's regime in the same legal category as Russians who had been resettled into Lithuania as part of Soviet colonisation policy.
The two sides eventually agreed on the neutral term "relocating persons" to cover both groups without equating them politically.
Finally, the thorniest question – whether Russia would accept responsibility for the 1940 annexation – was resolved not by the negotiating teams but by Landsbergis and Yeltsin personally.
"The Russian negotiators didn't want to accept responsibility for crimes committed by the Bolsheviks – all those acts of violence and coercion against neighbouring states. They didn't want the responsibility. Their position was that the Russian Federation, in restoring its own statehood, would not take on responsibility for the crimes of the communist regime," Stankevičius told LRT.lt.
Meanwhile, Landsbergis's own public position at the time was that responsibility lay with the USSR rather than Russia specifically.
So, the compromise text kept a reference to the 1940 annexation while dropping Lithuania's request to invoke an earlier, 1920 peace treaty in which Soviet Russia had renounced all claims to Lithuanian territory, making it's later Soviet occupation – illegal.
The irony
That compromise proved more significant than either side may have anticipated. When the Soviet Union collapsed months later, Russia inherited its rights and obligations as successor state – including, Lithuanian officials argue, responsibility for the consequences of the 1940 annexation that Russia itself had just agreed to acknowledge. And so, it was obliged to remedy the damage, withdraw its troops, and so on.
Three and a half decades on, the treaty's core value lies precisely in the fact that it is Moscow's own signature on a document that says the opposite of what the Kremlin now claims.

articles.title: Ukraine Wipes Out 75 Russian Drones Over Sumy, Including Rare $100,000 Knyaz Veschyi Oleg
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Wipes Out 75 Russian Drones Over Sumy, Including Rare $100,000 Knyaz Veschyi Oleg
Ukrainian air-defense drone operators have destroyed 75 Russian aerial targets over Sumy region since the beginning of August, including 53 Molniya-2 strike drones and a rare Knyaz Veschyi Oleg reconnaissance UAV valued at around $100,000.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade “Magura” reported on August 15 that its Sky Wars unit had intercepted 53 Molniya-2 drones, six ZALA Lancet loitering munitions, six FPV drones, three ZALA reconnaissance UAVs, three Gerbera drones, two drones identified as “Bombers,” one Knyaz Veschyi Oleg and one Mavic quadcopter.
Molniya-2s accounted for more than two-thirds of the total. The fixed-wing Russian FPV drone is designed as a relatively inexpensive platform for tactical strikes and reconnaissance.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the President of Ukraine on defense technology development, estimated its cost at about $1,600, putting the value of the 53 destroyed aircraft at roughly $84,800.
The six Lancets represent a significantly more expensive part of the losses. Developed by ZALA Aero, the Lancet family consists of loitering munitions used to locate and strike battlefield targets.
Beskrestnov estimated the newer X-52 at around $40,000 and the larger X-51 at about $68,000. Since the brigade did not specify the variants, the six destroyed Lancets could be worth approximately $240,000 to $408,000.
Among the rarest targets was the Knyaz Veschyi Oleg, a Russian tactical reconnaissance UAV developed by the Ushkuynik research and production center.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence lists it as having a 2.8-meter wingspan, endurance of up to 3.5 hours, an operational radius of around 45 kilometers and a maximum speed of 130 km/h. Ukrainian military units have previously valued the drone at approximately $100,000.
Sky Wars also destroyed three Gerbera drones. The Russian UAV is built largely from inexpensive materials and is commonly used as a decoy resembling Shahed-type attack drones, although reconnaissance and armed variants also exist.
Ukrainian estimates have placed its production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, giving the three destroyed Gerberas an estimated value of about $30,000.
The brigade did not specify the models of the three ZALA reconnaissance UAVs, six FPVs, two “Bombers,” or the Mavic, making their value difficult to determine reliably.
Based only on the 53 Molniya-2s, six Lancets, three Gerberas and the Knyaz Veschyi Oleg, the 63 identifiable drones had an estimated combined value of approximately $454,800 to $622,800. The real total for all 75 destroyed aircraft would therefore be higher.
Ukraine has also been pushing interceptor drones to greater altitudes. On August 2, border guards using a STING FPV interceptor destroyed a Russian ZALA Z-20 reconnaissance UAV at 6,858 meters over Chernihiv region, setting what Ukrainian authorities described as a world record for drone-on-drone interception.

articles.title: Should Iran negotiate with U.S. again?
articles.body:
In recent days, the Trump administration, after accepting undeniable defeats and bearing very heavy military costs, especially human casualties, has again leaned towards negotiations and agreements and, as in the past, is trying to convince Iran to negotiate by applying pressure and intimidation.
Iran believes that the goal of negotiations is to reach a common understanding acceptable to the negotiators and for the parties to adhere to the implementation of their commitments. In response to the invitation for negotiations from the United States, Iran accepted Pakistan's mediation, and detailed negotiations were held with good intentions and strong will at the level of the Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Iran's parliament) and the Vice President of the United States. This decision showed that Iran is determined to use diplomacy to secure the legitimate interests of the Iranian people, oppose war and tension, and end the oppressive sanctions.
The result of these negotiations led to the signing of a 14-point memorandum of understanding by the presidents of the two countries, with the assumption that Trump would respect his signature and adhere to the implementation of the memorandum's provisions. However, in practice, this did not happen, and the hostile moves of the United States with numerous attacks on southern Iran and the continuation of the naval blockade showed that the White House is not loyal to diplomacy and negotiations, but is also using this soft resource as a prelude to war and aggression.
Although the Islamic Republic of Iran welcomes diplomacy, it does not like the formula of negotiation for the sake of negotiation. Negotiations are valuable when they are aimed at achieving results and the parties are committed to implementing their commitments. At the current stage, there is no reason to conduct talks again, because in the previous negotiation, a memorandum of understanding was signed at the presidential level and is available. If for the United States, the invalidation of the president's signature does not matter, in Iran, the president's signature is valid and the provisions of the memorandum of understanding that was signed must be implemented to stop the war and resolve the remaining disputes.
Conducting negotiations to understand the demands and intentions of the other side was a logical and intelligent move, but today, not only Tehran but also many politicians around the world are skeptical about the seriousness of the American side in implementing the understandings and do not recommend repeating the failed negotiation. Of course, intermediary countries such as Pakistan and Qatar are active and convey messages, but conveying messages does not mean negotiating, and in the current situation, there is no desire and will on the Iranian side to negotiate with the United States. In fact, when the United States has failed in the test of negotiations and implementing the understandings, how can we talk about holding talks again?
The experience of negotiating several times with the United States shows that this country, due to its reliance on military, economic, and security power, only thinks about securing its own and Israel interests and wants immediate concessions from the other side and in return, only makes empty promises. The Islamic Republic of Iran, while being powerful, does not welcome war and tension, and at the same time does not accept the approach of negotiation for the sake of negotiation.

articles.title: Trump’s midterm malaise: endless war and high prices could spell doom for Republicans in November
articles.body:
He was always one step ahead. Donald Trump won the US presidency as a wildly unlikely outsider in 2016 and staged an astonishing comeback to win it again in 2024. Even his foes grudgingly called him a political savant with an intuition for exploiting grievances that left so-called experts floundering.
But now they are asking if the dark genius has lost his touch. Trump is trapped in the quagmire of an unpopular war, obsessing over monuments in Washington and looking for a new spokesperson after his White House press secretary quit. If the 80-year-old was deliberately trying to sabotage his Republican party in November’s midterm elections, it is not clear what he would do differently.
“He’s always had a reptilian political instinct for public opinion that has served him well,” said Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster. “You’re not seeing that much any more. You’re not seeing his ability to read the room. He seems tone-deaf on issues like the cost of living, the war, and the optics of gilding everything in sight and enshittifying Washington and he doesn’t care.”
Trump campaigned on promises to lower prices and keep the US out of foreign entanglements and forever wars. The opposite has happened. Voters say they are suffering a cost of living crisis, exacerbated by Trump’s sweeping tariffs. Buying food to eat at home has become 33% more expensive in US cities since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures.
Gas prices are at a record high for this time of year, in part thanks to the US war in Iran, which drags on with no end in sight. While Trump claims to have destroyed Iran’s military capabilities, it emerged this week that he was forced to hide in a catering truck and secretly swap planes after a Nato summit in Turkey because of a possible Iranian assassination plot.
The administration’s entanglement has metastasised into a gruelling, daily haemorrhage of resources, currently costing the taxpayer an estimated $1bn a day. Critics argue the administration has strengthened Iran’s resolve and provided it with global leverage, specifically over the strait of Hormuz. They see it as betrayal of the noninterventionist posture that fuelled Trump’s rise to power and attracted a generation of disaffected voters.
Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “What we’re watching right now is the complete unraveling of everything that Donald Trump, Maga and Republicans said they were about. They were against endless conflicts in the Middle East and they started a conflict in the Middle East without an exit strategy. They were supposed to be about no more spending American dollars abroad; we’re spending a billion dollars a day on this war without an end.”
Yet the president appears to have other, more aesthetic concerns. Since returning to power last year, the longtime property developer has invested much time and energy in construction projects across Washington, including a White House ballroom and helipad, a triumphal arch and an ill-fated makeover of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.
Bardella added: “As he continues this misadventure in the Middle East that has resulted in the cost of living going up, and continues to pour resources into putting his name on shit and building ballrooms and monuments to himself, the American people are going: what the fuck? That’s the only realistic reaction you could have when you objectively look at the circumstances.”
Trump’s second term has been defined by thinking big – Greenland, Venezuela, Iran – and thinking small. The board he appointed to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts added his name to the complex, only for a judge to order that it be removed; this week the board voted to add “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump” beneath the main sign.
According to Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, written by New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, the president has been seen with a tube of super glue trying to stick golden decorations to the marble fireplace in the Oval Office.
Haberman estimates that Trump now devotes 70% of his mental space to renovation projects and “monuments to self”. She told Axios’s Behind the Curtain video series that she and Swan visited Trump in the Oval Office in March. “You would think that on the 17th day of the war that he would have maps of the Middle East or maps of troop deployments – who knows,” she said. “He picks up these pictures, and [they’re] of maple trees, and he says: ‘I am choosing maple trees for the White House. I am good at picking trees.’ I’m paraphrasing here, but that is pretty much what he said.”
The president’s preoccupation with whether columns for his ballroom are more evocative of Athens or Rome, and with other efforts to preserve his legacy in marble, come as little surprise to Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill and longtime Trump critic.
She said: “Donald Trump has been an egomaniac, a narcissist his entire life. Even in the private sector he has slapped his name on buildings and a multitude of failed branding businesses from Trump steaks to Trump airline to Trump University to Trump water to Trump wine. Why is anyone surprised that he would take that same type of narcissism and bring it over to his role in his second-term as president when he’s spending other people’s money to do it?
“The problem has been that the Republican party has enabled him to get away with this and to their own detriment, which is why more and more people in his inner circle are concerned about how this is going to impact the midterms and control of Congress.”
Indeed, Republicans are said to be quietly panicking about Trump costing them the House of Representatives and putting even the Senate in jeopardy. A national Quinnipiac University Poll released late last month showed his job approval rating dropping to an all-time low of 32%, with 58% disapproval. It found six in 10 Americans oppose the US military action in Iran.
Past presidents such as George W Bush in 2006 and Barack Obama in 2010 have faced challenging midterms but worked with their parties in an effort to at least stem the losses. Rick Wilson, co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, said: “In both those cases their efforts were not successful, but it’s nightmarish to think what that would have been if Barack Obama had been saying, ‘I’m going to build a basketball arena at the White House,’ or George Bush had said, ‘I’m gonna build a golf course.’
“Instead you’ve got a very different visual from this White House and that visual is 'we don’t care about anything else except for the ballroom and the arch and all the throw-away ephemera that he wants to focus on. It’s a terrible political look and it’s quite dangerous for the party because they have nothing to run on right now.”
The sense of malaise deepened this week when Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary, announced that she will be stepping down at the end of the month. The official explanation was that the 28-year-old wants to spend more time with her young family but the timing was unfortunate for an administration struggling to spin its way out of one crisis after another.
For a president whose entire self-image is built on winning, the realisation that he is facing electoral defeat at home and humiliation abroad could be cause for an existential crisis. Sykes observed that, while Trump’s historical literacy is notoriously thin, he has begun to obsess over the ghosts of presidencies ruined by foreign blunders.
“It’s awfully interesting that in the Maggie Haberman book he’s comparing himself to Napoleon and Alexander the Great and Caesar but his deepest fear right now is that he’s going to be Herbert Hoover or Jimmy Carter,” he said.
Trump’s cloud does have a golden lining, however. He made an estimated $2.2bn during the first year of his second term thanks to cryptocurrency holdings, foreign interests and his Truth Social business.
Sykes added: “He hasn’t lowered the cost of living, he hasn’t made America more respected, he hasn’t won the war but he has succeeded in making himself a billionaire many times over by abusing his office.”

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday shared a glimpse of his morning routine, posting a video of himself feeding cows and peacocks before leaving for the Red Fort for India's 80th Independence Day celebrations.In a post on Instagram, Modi said feeding the animals was part of his daily routine and that they appeared to realise he was leaving earlier than usual for the Independence Day programme.

He was dressed in his traditional attire for the Independence Day celebrations.“Special, as always!” Modi said at the end of his post.The PM has also been increasingly active on Instagram in recent days, sharing selfie-style videos, personal reflections, GR and glimpses of his daily routine.The social media post offered a personal glimpse of the Prime Minister's morning ahead of the formal Independence Day programme, which included the flag-hoisting ceremony and his address to the nation.
Modi later reached the Red Fort, where he hoisted the national flag from the ramparts as part of the 80th Independence Day celebrations. The ceremony was accompanied by a 21-gun salute using indigenous 105 mm Light Field Guns.In his address, Modi outlined his government's priorities for India's development, with a focus on youth, manufacturing, technology, innovation and self-reliance. He also highlighted India's energy transition and plans to expand nuclear power capacity.The Prime Minister spoke about strengthening domestic manufacturing and reducing dependence on external sources, while highlighting sectors including defence, food processing, connectivity, green and blue economy and technology.
Youth development also featured prominently in his address, with Modi announcing measures linked to artificial intelligence training, innovation and competitive examinations.He also stressed the goal of building a Viksit Bharat by 2047, when India will mark 100 years of independence.The Independence Day programme additionally featured a rendition of Vande Mataram, with the national song completing 150 years this year.

articles.title: Drone illegally breaches Romania, F-18 fighter jet shoot it down
articles.body:
ALBAWABA - Romania’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that a drone illegally entered its airspace but was shot down by NATO.
According to the ministry's statement, a drone illegally breached Romania's national airspace, and it was destroyed by a Spanish F-18 fighter jet pilot at 05:01 a.m., CNN reported.
The F-18 jet "made radar contact with the target and received permission to engage it," the ministry revealed Sunday.
However, the source of the drone was unknown. However, this is not the first time a drone has breached Romania. Since the start of the war between Russia and Ukraine in 2022, several such incidents have taken place.
For instance, in July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots destroyed three Russian drones breaching the country's airspace.
The ministry only said that radars detected the drone coming from Moldova, some 24 km north of the southeastern Romanian city of Galati, according to CNN.
